title: Cloze Deletion
description: Flashcard type where key parts of a sentence are blanked for recall
body_head: # Cloze Deletion  ## Summary  Cloze deletion is a flashcard format where key parts of a sentence are blanked so the learner must supply them from context. It turns notes into recall prompts with minimal effort. It matters because it is the highest-yield card format for language, definitions, and fact learning. Cloze cards convert passive notes into active recall tasks at almost no authoring cost.  ## Details  - **Definition** — A cloze card presents a sentence with one or more gaps; the learner's task is to recall the missing text. - **Context preservation** — Keeping the full sentence preserves meaning and retrieval cues, unlike bare question-answer pairs. - **Multiple deletions** — Sever

title: Cognitive Flexibility
description: Capacity to shift between perspectives, tasks, or strategies
body_head: # Cognitive Flexibility  ## Summary  Cognitive Flexibility — Capacity to shift between perspectives, tasks, or strategies.  ## Details  - Cognitive flexibility is the executive ability to switch attention, perspectives, or strategies when conditions change — the 'shift' component alongside working-memory updating and inhibition. It is measured with task switching, set-shifting (Wisconsin Card Sort), and reversal-learning paradigms. - Flexibility supports learning: interleaved practice trains discrimination and shifting; rigid learners persist with obsolete strategies. It declines with stress, fatigue, and age, and improves with training and varied practice. - Worked example: a developer wh

title: Cognitive Load Theory
description: Instructional theory built on working-memory limits and schema-based long-term memory
body_head: # Cognitive Load Theory  ## Summary  Cognitive Load Theory — Instructional theory built on working-memory limits and schema-based long-term memory.  ## Details  - Cognitive load theory (Sweller) treats learning as schema acquisition in long-term memory, gated by a working memory with severe capacity limits. It distinguishes intrinsic load (imposed by the material's complexity), extraneous load (imposed by poor presentation), and germane load (devoted to schema construction). - Design principles follow: worked examples reduce extraneous load for novices, split-attention effects argue for integrated text-and-diagram, and redundancy warns against repeating the same information twice. The expe

title: Cognitive Offloading
description: Using the environment and tools to reduce internal cognitive demands
body_head: # Cognitive Offloading  ## Summary  Cognitive Offloading — Using the environment and tools to reduce internal cognitive demands.  ## Details  - Cognitive offloading is delegating memory, computation, or planning to the environment — notes, calculators, calendars, and external representations. It frees limited working memory and attention for higher-order reasoning, and is a defining feature of human tool use. - Research shows people offload strategically: when a task strains memory, they write more; reminders and external stores improve performance but can create dependence (the 'Google effect' — remembering where information is stored rather than the content). - Worked example: a knowledg

title: Collective Intelligence
description: Group capacity to solve problems that exceeds any individual member
body_head: # Collective Intelligence  ## Summary  Collective Intelligence — Group capacity to solve problems that exceeds any individual member.  ## Details  - Collective intelligence is the capability of groups to think, decide, and create beyond what individuals could alone. It depends on composition, interaction, and aggregation: diverse independent judgments (the wisdom of crowds), structured deliberation, and tools that combine contributions. - Conditions matter: independence and diversity prevent herding; aggregation rules beat unstructured discussion (Galton's ox, prediction markets); social influence can destroy or amplify accuracy; and groupthink degrades judgment without dissent mechanisms.

title: Concept Formation
description: How categories and abstract ideas are built from examples and experience
body_head: # Concept Formation  ## Summary  Concept Formation — How categories and abstract ideas are built from examples and experience.  ## Details  - Concept formation is the process of constructing categories — birds, fairness, quadratic equations — from encounters with examples, features, and feedback. Accounts differ: classical (necessary and sufficient features), prototype (central tendency), exemplar (stored instances), and theory-based (causal and explanatory structure) views all capture parts of the evidence. - Empirical findings: typicality effects (robins are more central than penguins), family resemblance, and the importance of contrasting examples in learning boundaries. Learners acquir

title: Concept Map Research
description: Studies on concept maps as learning, assessment, and knowledge-organization tools
body_head: # Concept Map Research  ## Summary  Concept Map Research — Studies on concept maps as learning, assessment, and knowledge-organization tools. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Concept maps represent knowledge as labeled nodes and linking phrases. - Research shows benefits for meaningful learning when students construct, not just copy, maps. - Used as assessment: map structure correlates with expert knowledge organization. - Novak's work anchors the field; digital tools make maps live artifacts.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/concept-mapping|Concept Mapping]] — the mykb article - [[wiki/memory/knowledge-map-research|

title: Concept Mapping
description: Diagram that links concepts with labeled relations to expose a domain's structure
body_head: # Concept Mapping  ## Summary Concept mapping goes beyond mind maps by labeling the edges: 'spaced repetition *increases* retention'. It externalizes the relational structure of a topic and makes gaps visible. Where a mind map shows association, a concept map shows a claim — and claims are what a knowledge base should record.  ## Details - **Parts** — concept nodes, labeled directed edges, and cross-links between branches; propositions are node-edge-node triples. A map of "forgetting" might contain: retrieval practice *strengthens* memory traces; interference *weakens* traces; sleep *consolidates* traces — each edge is a testable proposition. - **Use** — assessment, learning design, and pl

title: Conceptual Change
description: Deep restructuring of concepts rather than mere accretion of facts
body_head: # Conceptual Change  ## Summary  Conceptual Change — Deep restructuring of concepts rather than mere accretion of facts.  ## Details  - Conceptual change is the transformation of a learner's core concepts — for example, replacing a folk theory of motion with Newtonian mechanics. It contrasts with accretion, where new facts fit existing structures; change requires the old framework to be revised or abandoned. - Research shows naive conceptions are coherent, functional, and stubborn: they resist instruction because they explain everyday experience well. Effective change requires confrontation with anomalies, intelligible alternatives, and motivation to revise. - Worked example: a student bel

title: Constructive Episodic Simulation
description: Theory that memory recombines episodic details to simulate the future
body_head: # Constructive Episodic Simulation  ## Summary  Constructive Episodic Simulation — Theory that memory recombines episodic details to simulate the future. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Schacter & Addis: episodic memory is constructive, flexibly recombining stored details. - The same constructive machinery builds remembered pasts and imagined futures. - Explains memory errors as a byproduct of flexibility rather than pure storage failure. - Frames memory as forward-looking: it exists to simulate and predict.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/episodic-future-thinking|Episodic Future Thinking]] — application - [[wiki/m

title: Context-Dependent Memory
description: Better recall when the environment matches the encoding environment
body_head: # Context-Dependent Memory  ## Summary  Context-Dependent Memory — Better recall when the environment matches the encoding environment.  ## Details  - Context-dependent memory is the finding that retrieval improves when the external context matches encoding — same room, same music, same smells. Godden & Baddeley's classic study had divers learn words either underwater or on land; recall was best when study and test environments matched. - The effect is cue-based: contextual features get bound into the trace and act as retrieval cues. It is robust for free recall, weaker for recognition, and strongest when contexts are distinctive. - Worked example: students who study for an exam in the exa

title: Cornell Notes
description: Two-column note format with a cue column, note area, and summary row for active review
body_head: # Cornell Notes  ## Summary Cornell Notes split each page into a narrow cue column, a wide note area, and a bottom summary band. The cue column doubles as a self-test prompt, turning passive notes into an active-recall device: cover the note area, answer the cues, then verify. It is one of the few note formats that builds retrieval practice into the page layout itself.  ## Details - **Layout** — main notes on the right (lectures, readings, sessions); questions/keywords on the left; a one-paragraph summary at the bottom written in your own words. The cue column is populated after the fact, ideally by converting each chunk of the note area into a question the chunk answers. - **Review loop**

title: Counterfactual Reasoning
description: Imagining alternatives to what happened, 'what if' thinking
body_head: # Counterfactual Reasoning  ## Summary  Counterfactual Reasoning — Imagining alternatives to what happened, 'what if' thinking.  ## Details  - Counterfactual reasoning generates alternatives to reality: what if I had studied harder, what if the patient's blood pressure had been checked. It underpins causal judgment (X caused Y if Y would not have occurred without X), blame and credit assignment, regret, and learning from experience. - Mental simulation of alternatives is effortful and selective: people mutate the most controllable and abnormal elements of the situation, which shapes hindsight, blame, and counterfactual emotions like regret and relief. - Worked example: after a project fail

title: Decay Theory
description: Forgetting as the fading of memory traces over time
body_head: # Decay Theory  ## Summary  Decay Theory — Forgetting as the fading of memory traces over time. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Oldest account of forgetting: traces weaken with disuse unless rehearsed. - Hard to test cleanly because time correlates with interference and context change. - Modern versions survive in time-based accounts of working-memory loss. - Complements interference-theory; both shape the forgetting-curve.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/interference-theory|Interference Theory]] — rival and complement - [[wiki/memory/forgetting-curve|Forgetting Curve]] — the phenomenon theories explain - [[wiki/me

title: Delay of Gratification
description: Choosing larger later rewards over smaller immediate ones
body_head: # Delay of Gratification  ## Summary  Delay of Gratification — Choosing larger later rewards over smaller immediate ones. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Mischel's marshmallow paradigm measured preschool delay ability and its longitudinal correlates. - Reanalysis suggests family background explains much of the apparent predictive power. - Delay improves with age, strategy use, and trust in the delayed reward. - Modeled in decision theory as temporal discounting.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/self-control-research|Self-Control Research]] — field home - [[wiki/concepts/decision-theory|Decision Theory]] — formal mod

title: Deliberate Practice
description: Structured, goal-directed practice with immediate feedback aimed at the edge of ability
body_head: # Deliberate Practice  ## Summary  Deliberate Practice — Structured, goal-directed practice with immediate feedback aimed at the edge of ability.  ## Details  - Deliberate practice (Ericsson) is training designed specifically to improve performance: tasks at the edge of current ability, clear goals, immediate feedback, and repeated refinement. It is distinguished from mere experience or naive repetition, which plateaus quickly. - Key features: a coach or design specifies the task, attention is fully engaged, errors are diagnosed and corrected, and sessions are limited by concentration. Domain after domain — music, chess, sport, medicine — accumulated deliberate practice tracks expert perfo

title: Desirable Difficulties
description: Conditions that slow initial learning but improve long-term retention and transfer
body_head: # Desirable Difficulties  ## Summary  Desirable Difficulties — Conditions that slow initial learning but improve long-term retention and transfer.  ## Details  - Desirable difficulties are study conditions that make initial performance harder or slower while improving durable learning. Bjork's list includes spacing, interleaving, retrieval practice, generation, and varied practice contexts. - The mechanism: harder processing at encoding produces richer, more flexible traces; fluency during study is a poor predictor of later retrieval. The catch is that both learners and teachers misread difficulty as failure, abandoning the very conditions that work. - Worked example: struggling to recall

title: Digit Span Test
description: Classic working-memory measure: repeat back digit sequences of increasing length
body_head: # Digit Span Test  ## Summary  Digit Span Test — Classic working-memory measure: repeat back digit sequences of increasing length. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Forward span measures storage; backward span adds manipulation, a better WM indicator. - Typical adult forward span is 7±2 digits; backward span is usually 1-2 fewer. - Central to intelligence batteries and a standard lab measure of short-term storage. - Links to working-memory-capacity and chunk-size-effects.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/working-memory-capacity|Working Memory Capacity]] — what the test samples - [[wiki/memory/chunk-size-effects|Chunk

title: Digital Garden Practice
description: Publishing notes in progressive states of maturity instead of finished posts
body_head: # Digital Garden Practice  ## Summary  Digital Garden Practice — Publishing notes in progressive states of maturity instead of finished posts. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Gardens grow: seeds (stubs) become seedlings, then evergreens, through public iteration. - Emphasizes linking, revision dates, and partial completion over polished outputs. - Creates accountability and reuse pressure that improve note quality. - mykb's status field is a private version of the same maturity gradient.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/digital-garden|Digital Garden]] — existing article - [[wiki/memory/evergreen-note-taking|Evergree

title: Digital Garden
description: Public or semi-public personal wiki of evergreen notes that grow through iteration
body_head: # Digital Garden  ## Summary A digital garden is a personal knowledge base published as a web of linked, evolving notes — part blog, part wiki, part notebook. Notes are seeds or seedlings first, then mature through repeated revision, which values process over polish: the garden is never finished, and each note's history is part of its value.  ## Details - **Metaphor** — seeds (raw ideas) grow into seedlings (drafts) and then evergreens (stable, linked notes); nothing is finished, everything is tended. A garden with only seeds is a messy inbox; a garden with only evergreens is a blog in disguise. The lifecycle is what makes the garden a *practice* rather than a publication. - **Contrast wit

title: Distributed Cognition
description: Cognition spread across people, tools, and environments
body_head: # Distributed Cognition  ## Summary  Distributed Cognition — Cognition spread across people, tools, and environments.  ## Details  - Distributed cognition treats cognitive processes as spread across individuals, artifacts, and social arrangements — a cockpit crew with instruments, or a design team with whiteboards — rather than contained in single heads. Hutchins' studies of ship navigation showed that the task's cognitive work is done by the whole system. - The framework analyzes information flow, representational states, and coordination; the unit of analysis is the system, and cognition is observed in its transformations and propagations. - Worked example: navigating a ship uses the hel

title: Documentation Practices
description: Habits and standards for writing durable, findable documentation
body_head: # Documentation Practices  ## Summary  Documentation Practices — Habits and standards for writing durable, findable documentation. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Good docs have clear scope, stable identifiers, and examples that outlive the author's memory. - Practices include style guides, templates, changelogs, and review ownership. - Documentation is externalized knowledge with a maintenance schedule attached. - mykb applies this at wiki scale: frontmatter, tags, and link discipline are documentation practices.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/externalization-of-knowledge|Externalization of Knowledge]] — what doc

title: Dual Coding Theory
description: Paivio's account of memory through separate verbal and imagery systems
body_head: # Dual Coding Theory  ## Summary  Dual Coding Theory — Paivio's account of memory through separate verbal and imagery systems.  ## Details  - Dual coding theory (Paivio) proposes two interconnected systems: a verbal system for language and a nonverbal (imagery) system for objects and scenes. Information encoded in both systems is remembered better than information in one, because either system can cue the other at retrieval. - Concrete words (dog, apple) are dually coded automatically; abstract words (justice, truth) lean on verbal coding alone, which is one reason concrete material is easier to learn. The imagery advantage is strongest for paired-associate and vocabulary learning. - Worke

title: Elaborative Interrogation
description: Asking why questions to connect new facts with existing knowledge
body_head: # Elaborative Interrogation  ## Summary  Elaborative Interrogation — Asking why questions to connect new facts with existing knowledge.  ## Details  - Elaborative interrogation is a learning strategy: after reading a fact, ask 'why is this true?' and generate an explanation. The act forces the learner to connect the new fact to prior knowledge, creating elaborated, distinctive memory traces. - Research consistently shows benefits over repetition and note-taking for fact learning, with moderate effect sizes; the effect is strongest when learners have relevant background knowledge to draw on, and it transfers to delayed tests. - Worked example: studying 'the Sahara was once green' → ask why

title: Embodied Cognition
description: Cognition shaped by the body's morphology, sensorimotor systems, and action
body_head: # Embodied Cognition  ## Summary  Embodied Cognition — Cognition shaped by the body's morphology, sensorimotor systems, and action.  ## Details  - Embodied cognition claims that thinking is grounded in bodily experience: perception, action, and the body's constraints shape concepts, memory, and reasoning. Evidence includes sensorimotor grounding of abstract concepts, gesture facilitating thought, and action-compatible effects on judgment. - Strong versions argue cognition is constituted by body-world interaction; weaker versions hold that simulation and bodily states heavily influence, but do not constitute, thought. The debate is active, with replication of some flagship effects contested

title: Emotional Regulation
description: Processes by which people influence which emotions they have and how they express them
body_head: # Emotional Regulation  ## Summary  Emotional Regulation — Processes by which people influence which emotions they have and how they express them. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Gross's process model: situation selection, modification, attention, reappraisal, and suppression. - Reappraisal generally beats suppression for well-being and memory outcomes. - Regulation skill predicts social, academic, and health outcomes. - Pairs with mood-congruent memory and test-anxiety research.  ## Related  - [[wiki/meta-learning/test-anxiety|Test Anxiety]] — emotion in performance settings - [[wiki/memory/mood-congruent-memor

title: Encoding-Retrieval Match
description: The principle that retrieval benefits from overlap with encoding conditions
body_head: # Encoding-Retrieval Match  ## Summary  The encoding-retrieval match principle states that retrieval succeeds when the conditions at recall overlap with the conditions at encoding. Context, cues, and internal state all form part of that match. It matters because it explains both why context-dependent memory works and how to design better retrieval practice. The principle is a design rule: build the retrieval cue into the way the material was learned.  ## Details  - **Definition** — Memory is strongest when the cues present during retrieval resemble those present when the memory was encoded. - **Context dependence** — Environment, mood, and internal state become part of the memory trace, ai

title: Encoding Specificity
description: Tulving's principle: retrieval succeeds when cues match encoding conditions
body_head: # Encoding Specificity  ## Summary  Encoding Specificity — Tulving's principle: retrieval succeeds when cues match encoding conditions.  ## Details  - Encoding specificity (Tulving) states that what is stored includes the context and cues present at encoding, and retrieval succeeds when the test reinstates those cues. Memory is not a store of context-free traces; it is a record of cue-trace associations. - Evidence: recognition failure of recallable words (words free-recalled but not recognized), context-dependent memory effects, and the superiority of identical study-test cues. The principle explains why transfer-appropriate processing works and why reinstating study context helps. - Work

title: Environmental Reinstatement
description: Returning to the physical environment of learning to cue recall
body_head: # Environmental Reinstatement  ## Summary  Environmental Reinstatement — Returning to the physical environment of learning to cue recall. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Godden & Baddeley's diving study: recall was best when study and test environments matched. - Environmental cues are strongest for incidental details; benefits can be modest in real classrooms.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/context-dependent-memory|Context Dependent Memory]] — umbrella effect - [[wiki/memory/reinstatement-of-context|Reinstatement of Context]] — mental variant - [[wiki/memory/encoding-specificity|Encoding Specificity]] — theoretic

title: Episodic Future Thinking
description: Imagining specific future events using the episodic memory system
body_head: # Episodic Future Thinking  ## Summary  Episodic future thinking is the capacity to imagine specific, plausible future events using the same constructive machinery that recalls past experiences. It is not generic forecasting; it produces scene-like simulations with people, places, and timelines. This matters because these mental simulations guide planning, motivate goal pursuit, and shape decisions about delayed rewards.  ## Details  - **Definition** — episodic future thinking projects the self into a particular future moment, constructing a detailed event rather than abstract expectation. - **Constructive mechanism** — the theory of constructive episodic simulation holds that memory provi

title: Evergreen Note-Taking
description: Writing durable notes that are independently meaningful and develop over time
body_head: # Evergreen Note-Taking  ## Summary  Evergreen Note-Taking — Writing durable notes that are independently meaningful and develop over time. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Evergreen notes are written for permanence: standalone, title-like-a-claim, revision-friendly. - They are maintained, not collected — editing matters as much as capturing. - Andy Matuschak's framing ties them to spaced repetition and writing as thinking. - mykb's growing/stub statuses mirror the evergreen lifecycle.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/evergreen-notes|Evergreen Notes]] — existing article - [[wiki/memory/atomic-notes-practice|Atomic No

title: Evergreen Notes
description: Atomic, linked, and written in your own words so they can be reused across many future contexts
body_head: # Evergreen Notes  ## Summary Evergreen notes are atomic, linked, and written in your own words so they can be reused across many future contexts. They are the core unit of modern personal knowledge management and the target state of a digital garden: stable titles, precise claims, and enough connection to the rest of the network that any future project can assemble them instead of re-deriving the knowledge.  ## Details - **Properties** — one idea, own words, precise title, links to related notes, and maintenance over time. The title is a claim or noun phrase that names the idea ("Attention is a queueing problem" beats "Attention notes"); the body commits to the claim and revises as unders

title: Expectancy Effects
description: Prior expectations shaping perception, memory, and performance
body_head: # Expectancy Effects  ## Summary  Expectancy Effects — Prior expectations shaping perception, memory, and performance. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Expectations guide attention and interpretation, producing confirmation-prone processing. - In memory, expected events are reconstructed rather than remembered verbatim. - Expectancy also drives placebo and experimenter effects in performance research. - Overlaps with schema effects and top-down processing.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/memory-schema-effects|Memory Schema Effects]] — schema-based memory - [[wiki/concepts/top-down-processing|Top-Down Processing]] —

title: Extended Mind
description: Clark and Chalmers' claim that external resources can constitute mental processes
body_head: # Extended Mind  ## Summary  Extended Mind — Clark and Chalmers' claim that external resources can constitute mental processes.  ## Details  - The extended mind thesis (Clark & Chalmers) argues that some external resources — notebooks, phones, or a wiki — can be parts of the cognitive system, not merely instruments. If a resource is reliably coupled, serves the same function as internal memory, and is available without deliberation, it is as much a vehicle of cognition as a brain trace. - The famous parity argument: Otto with Alzheimer's uses a notebook as his memory; Inga uses biological memory; functionally the notebook does memory work and should count as part of Otto's mind. Critics di

title: Externalization of Knowledge
description: Encoding knowledge into durable external artifacts such as notes, docs, and models
body_head: # Externalization of Knowledge  ## Summary  Externalization of Knowledge — Encoding knowledge into durable external artifacts such as notes, docs, and models. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - External memory extends internal recall and frees working-memory capacity. - Artifacts create provenance, reviewability, and shareability that internal memory lacks. - Externalization is the core operation of a personal knowledge management system like mykb. - Quality depends on structure: atomic notes, typed links, and metadata.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/knowledge-articulation|Knowledge Articulation]] — the act that prec

title: False Memory Formation
description: Remembering events that did not happen, or differently than they did
body_head: # False Memory Formation  ## Summary  False Memory Formation — Remembering events that did not happen, or differently than they did.  ## Details  - False memories are recollections of events that never occurred, or of details that differ from reality. They arise from the same constructive machinery as true memories: imagination, suggestion, schema-based filling-in, and source-monitoring failures combine to produce confident, detailed fabrications. - Landmark demonstrations: Loftus's lost-in-the-mall studies (plausible implanted memories), Deese-Roediger-McDermott lists (false recall of non-presented associates), and imagination inflation (imagining raises belief that it happened). - Worked

title: Flashbulb Memory
description: Vivid, detailed recollections of learning about shocking public events
body_head: # Flashbulb Memory  ## Summary  Flashbulb Memory — Vivid, detailed recollections of learning about shocking public events. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - People believe these memories are photographic, but research shows they decay like other memories. - Confidence stays high while accuracy drops — a vividness-accuracy dissociation. - Now understood as ordinary autobiographical memory boosted by emotion, rehearsal, and novelty. - Useful caution for source-memory and misinformation research.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/autobiographical-memory|Autobiographical Memory]] — system flashbulbs belong to - [[wiki/memo

title: Flashcard Design
description: Principles for writing flashcards that trigger retrieval instead of recognition
body_head: # Flashcard Design  ## Summary Flashcard design is the craft of writing prompts that trigger retrieval instead of recognition: each card tests one specific fact, gives no answer-side cues, and is hard enough to strengthen the memory but fair enough to answer from what you know. A well-designed card is a tiny retrieval-practice event; a poorly designed one is a puzzle or a triviality.  ## Details - Cards should be atomic: one prompt, one answer, no compound questions. "What are the failure modes of X?" is not one card — it is a list that lets recognition of the first item stand in for recall of the rest. Split it into one card per failure mode. - Avoid cloze overuse and answer-side cues tha

title: Folksonomy
description: User-generated, flat tagging of items that emerges bottom-up instead of from a controlled hierarchy
body_head: # Folksonomy  ## Summary A folksonomy is classification by free-form tags applied by users (or agents), forming a flat, emergent vocabulary. It is cheap to create, adapts to how people actually describe things, and powers retrieval without a curated hierarchy. Its cost is ambiguity: synonyms, plurals, and inconsistent tagging dilute precision.  ## Details - **Emergence** — tags aggregate into co-occurrence networks; 'popular tags' views emerge from usage rather than authority. - **Strengths** — zero setup, captures multiple perspectives, adapts quickly to new domains; ideal for personal notes and small teams. - **Weaknesses** — no synonym control (memory/remembrance), no hierarchy, tag spa

title: Forgetting Curve
description: The exponential decline of memory strength over time without review
body_head: # Forgetting Curve  ## Summary  Forgetting Curve — The exponential decline of memory strength over time without review.  ## Details  - The forgetting curve describes how rapidly learned material fades when it is not retrieved. Ebbinghaus's original curves showed steep loss within hours and days, followed by a flattening tail; later work shows the decline is approximately exponential and highly sensitive to encoding strength and review. - Key factors: initial learning strength (overlearning and elaboration flatten the curve), interference from similar material, and retrieval events — each successful recall resets and flattens the curve, which is exactly what spaced repetition exploits. - Wo

title: Forward Models
description: Internal models that predict the sensory consequences of actions
body_head: # Forward Models  ## Summary Forward models predict the sensory outcome of an action before it happens, enabling fast correction and distinguishing self-caused from external sensations. They are central to motor control and to perceiving agency. Prediction failures produce surprises and symptoms.  ## Details - **Use** — efference copy and sensory prediction. - **Agency** — matching predictions mark self-generated events. - **In mykb** — expected-outcome logs are forward models.  ## Related - [[wiki/memory/internal-models|Internal Models]] — the family - [[wiki/memory/inverse-models|Inverse Models]] — the complementary function - [[wiki/memory/motor-learning|Motor Learning]] — acquiring the

title: Generation Effect
description: Producing information oneself improves memory more than reading it
body_head: # Generation Effect  ## Summary  Generation Effect — Producing information oneself improves memory more than reading it.  ## Details  - The generation effect is the finding that self-generated information is remembered better than identical information that is merely read. Slamecka and Graf demonstrated it with word fragments ('c-a-? → cat'), and it extends to answers, examples, and summaries. - Explanations emphasize deeper semantic processing, stronger item-specific encoding, and the effort of producing the response. The effect persists across delays and pairs with the testing effect because both route learning through active production. - Worked example: completing a sentence 'Anki uses

title: Generative Models
description: Models that can produce data or predictions, central to predictive and model-based accounts
body_head: # Generative Models  ## Summary Generative models capture how data are produced, enabling prediction and simulation of outcomes. The brain is thought to run generative models of the world, and AI systems use them for generation and planning. They contrast with discriminative models that only classify.  ## Details - **Function** — predict and simulate; support planning. - **Cognitive role** — world models are generative. - **In mykb** — explicit models enable counterfactual reasoning.  ## Related - [[wiki/memory/predictive-processing|Predictive Processing]] — the cognitive use - [[wiki/memory/model-based-cognition|Model-Based Cognition]] — planning with models - [[wiki/concepts/world-models

title: Gist Extraction
description: Reducing material to its central meaning while discarding surface detail
body_head: # Gist Extraction  ## Summary  Gist Extraction — Reducing material to its central meaning while discarding surface detail. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Gist is the semantic core; it is more durable and more transferable than verbatim detail. - Fuzzy-trace theory contrasts verbatim and gist memory traces. - Summarizing is the active version: extracting gist forces selection and connection. - mykb relevance: captures become gist-first notes, with details attached as needed.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/summarization-cognition|Summarization Cognition]] — the cognitive process - [[wiki/memory/schema-theory|Schema

title: Git for Notes
description: Using git version control for note repositories to get history, diffs, and rollback
body_head: # Git for Notes  ## Summary Git for notes means keeping a markdown knowledge base in a git repository so every change has history, authorship, and rollback. It gives a wiki the safety net that databases get from transactions: nothing is ever truly lost, every edit can be diffed and reviewed, and mistakes can be reverted to the last good state.  ## Details - **What you get** — full history, `git diff` for review, rollback on mistakes, and branching for experiments. A wiki with git can treat each curation pass as a commit, so the question "what did last week's consolidation change?" has a precise answer rather than a memory. - **Costs** — merge conflicts on concurrent edits and binary blobs;

title: Graph Notes
description: Practice of managing notes as a graph where links define structure instead of folders
body_head: # Graph Notes  ## Summary Graph notes treat a note collection as a network: pages are nodes, links are edges, and structure emerges from connectivity rather than folders. The graph view exposes clusters, bridges, and orphans that folders hide, turning the act of linking into the primary organizing activity instead of a secondary decoration.  ## Details - **Graph view** — nodes cluster by link density; communities of related ideas become visible at a glance. A well-linked wiki shows dense clusters for each topic area, with a few high-degree hubs (concepts like "spaced repetition" or "schema migrations") bridging clusters — and these hubs are exactly the notes worth writing well. - **Benefit

title: Grit Research
description: Study of perseverance and passion for long-term goals
body_head: # Grit Research  ## Summary  Grit Research — Study of perseverance and passion for long-term goals. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Duckworth's grit predicts achievement in some domains beyond talent and IQ. - Critiques: high overlap with conscientiousness and weak incremental validity in many samples. - Perseverance matters, but strategy, practice quality, and context may matter more. - Related to deliberate practice and to growth-oriented motivation research.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/deliberate-practice|Deliberate Practice]] — quality-of-effort link - [[wiki/meta-learning/task-persistence|Task Persistence]

title: Habit vs Goal-Directed Control
description: Dual systems of action: automatic stimulus-response habits vs deliberative goals
body_head: # Habit vs Goal-Directed Control  ## Summary  Habit vs Goal-Directed Control — Dual systems of action: automatic stimulus-response habits vs deliberative goals. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Habits run on stimulus-response associations; goal-directed control uses model-based evaluation. - With overtraining, behavior shifts from goal-directed to habitual, resistant to outcome change. - Stress and load bias the system toward habit. - Modeled computationally as model-free vs model-based reinforcement learning.  ## Related  - [[wiki/meta-learning/model-free-learning|Model-Free Learning]] — computational account -

title: Handwritten vs Typed Notes
description: Whether pen or keyboard better supports encoding and later recall
body_head: # Handwritten vs Typed Notes  ## Summary  Handwritten vs Typed Notes — Whether pen or keyboard better supports encoding and later recall. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Studies (e.g., Mueller & Oppenheimer) found handwritten notes improve conceptual performance, partly due to more paraphrase and less verbatim capture. - Typing wins on speed and searchability; losses come from shallower processing, not the medium itself. - Best practice may be typed capture plus handwritten-style elaboration and review. - The encoding-retrieval match matters more than the medium.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/note-taking-research

title: Hindsight Bias
description: Seeing past events as more predictable than they were
body_head: # Hindsight Bias  ## Summary  Hindsight Bias — Seeing past events as more predictable than they were.  ## Details  - Hindsight bias — the 'I knew it all along' effect — is the tendency to overestimate, after an outcome is known, how predictable it was in advance. It distorts memory of one's own prior predictions and inflates the perceived obviousness of outcomes. - Mechanisms: outcome knowledge automatically updates the causal story (creeping determinism), and memory reconstruction pulls prior beliefs toward the known outcome. It is robust across domains — politics, medicine, sports, finance — and survives expertise. - Worked example: after a project fails, team members recall being more w

title: Imagination and Memory
description: Shared cognitive machinery for imagining events and remembering them
body_head: # Imagination and Memory  ## Summary  Imagination and Memory — Shared cognitive machinery for imagining events and remembering them. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Imagination and memory recruit overlapping hippocampal and default-mode networks. - Imagining an event can later be mistaken for a memory of it — the imagination inflation effect. - Imagination also serves episodic future thinking and counterfactual reasoning. - A key caution for eyewitness and false-memory research.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/constructive-episodic-simulation|Constructive Episodic Simulation]] — shared machinery account - [[wiki/me

title: Incremental Reading
description: Reading texts progressively through spaced, extractable chunks
body_head: # Incremental Reading  ## Summary  Incremental Reading — Reading texts progressively through spaced, extractable chunks. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Developed in SuperMemo: readings are broken into excerpts that appear on a spaced schedule. - Readers extract, reformulate, and convert passages into cards as they go. - Turns a linear text into a personalized, memory-driven curriculum. - Demands strong card hygiene to avoid an unmanageable queue.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/anki-workflow|Anki Workflow]] — digital sibling - [[wiki/memory/spaced-memorization|Spaced Memorization]] — the schedule - [[wiki/memory/c

title: Information Architecture
description: Design of how information is organized, labeled, and navigated in a system
body_head: # Information Architecture  ## Summary Information architecture (IA) is the discipline of structuring, labeling, and interlinking content so users (or agents) can find what they need. It covers navigation schemes, naming conventions, and the mental model a system presents — and in a wiki, IA is what separates a searchable knowledge base from a pile of markdown files.  ## Details - **Components** — organization systems (taxonomies, faceted classification), labeling systems (titles, tags, frontmatter fields), navigation (indexes, links, backlinks), and search. All four must agree: a page labeled one way in navigation and another way in search is a page users cannot find. - **Principles** — p

title: Interference Theory
description: Forgetting caused by competing memories rather than simple decay
body_head: # Interference Theory  ## Summary  Interference Theory — Forgetting caused by competing memories rather than simple decay. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - New learning disrupts old memories (retroactive) and old learning disrupts new (proactive). - Evidence includes paired-associate experiments where similar lists collide. - Interference explains why similar material is harder to keep separate than dissimilar material. - Central to forgetting-curve and spaced-repetition-systems design.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/proactive-interference|Proactive Interference]] — old-on-new direction - [[wiki/memory/retroactive-

title: Interleaved Practice
description: Mixing different topics or problem types within a practice session
body_head: # Interleaved Practice  ## Summary  Interleaved Practice — Mixing different topics or problem types within a practice session.  ## Details  - Interleaved practice alternates between different topics or problem types within one session, rather than blocking them. It reliably improves test performance, especially on mixed, transfer, and delayed assessments, even though it feels harder and less fluent during practice. - Mechanisms: interleaving forces discrimination between problem types, reactivates earlier material (spacing-like benefit), and prevents the mindless application of a single just-seen procedure. - Worked example: a math student who alternates quadratic, exponential, and logarit

title: Internal Models
description: Stored representations of how the world, body, or others behave
body_head: # Internal Models  ## Summary Internal models are the brain's stored representations of regularities — of the body, environment, and other minds — used for prediction and control. Forward models predict outcomes of actions; inverse models compute required actions. They are learned and continuously updated.  ## Details - **Types** — forward and inverse models. - **Functions** — prediction, control, and simulation. - **In mykb** — documented models support debugging of reasoning.  ## Related - [[wiki/memory/forward-models|Forward Models]] — predicting outcomes - [[wiki/memory/inverse-models|Inverse Models]] — computing actions - [[wiki/memory/model-based-cognition|Model-Based Cognition]] — t

title: Inverse Models
description: Internal models that compute the actions needed to reach desired outcomes
body_head: # Inverse Models  ## Summary Inverse models compute the motor or cognitive commands required to achieve a desired state — the inverse of forward prediction. They enable goal-directed action and are learned through practice. They pair with forward models in control architectures.  ## Details - **Function** — desired state to required action. - **Learning** — refined by error correction over practice. - **In mykb** — procedures are inverse models for goals.  ## Related - [[wiki/memory/forward-models|Forward Models]] — the predictive pair - [[wiki/memory/internal-models|Internal Models]] — the family - [[wiki/memory/motor-learning|Motor Learning]] — the acquisition - [[wiki/memory/model-based

title: Just-in-Time Learning
description: Learning a skill or fact exactly when a task requires it rather than in advance
body_head: # Just-in-Time Learning  ## Summary Just-in-time learning delays study until the moment of need: look up the API, technique, or fact while doing the task, apply it immediately, and retain the part that worked. It optimizes for throughput over scheduled mastery — you learn what the task actually demands, right when the task demands it.  ## Details - **Trade-off** — immediate relevance and low overhead vs shallow, context-dependent retention; complements rather than replaces deliberate practice. Facts learned only in context are recalled mainly in that context, which is why just-in-time learning must be paired with a system that re-surfaces the same fact later (spaced repetition or wiki retr

title: Keyword Method
description: Vocabulary mnemonic linking a foreign word to a similar-sounding keyword image
body_head: # Keyword Method  ## Summary  Keyword Method — Vocabulary mnemonic linking a foreign word to a similar-sounding keyword image. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Find a keyword in your language that sounds like the target word, then picture them interacting. - Example: Spanish 'pato' (duck) → keyword 'pot' → image of a duck in a pot. - Meta-analyses show it reliably improves immediate and delayed vocabulary recall. - Works best for concrete, imageable keywords; less useful for abstract terms.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/mnemonic-techniques|Mnemonic Techniques]] — core technique family - [[wiki/memory/dual-coding-t

title: Knowledge Articulation
description: Making tacit understanding explicit through language, diagrams, or explanation
body_head: # Knowledge Articulation  ## Summary  Knowledge Articulation — Making tacit understanding explicit through language, diagrams, or explanation. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Articulation forces knowledge from implicit to explicit form, exposing gaps. - Writing, teaching, and diagramming are the main articulation channels. - Links to self-explanation and to knowledge-externalization as its durable output. - mykb relevance: wiki articles are articulated knowledge; stubs mark where articulation is thin.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/externalization-of-knowledge|Externalization of Knowledge]] — the durable output -

title: Knowledge Capture
description: The act of getting external information into a knowledge system while it is still fresh
body_head: # Knowledge Capture  ## Summary Knowledge capture is the front end of every knowledge loop: turning an experience, reading, or conversation into a durable record. Good capture lowers friction so nothing valuable is lost; bad capture produces an unsearchable pile. The test of capture is not whether something was recorded — it is whether the record can be found and used later.  ## Details - **Design** — a low-friction inbox (drop anything, tag lightly, move on); processing happens later, not at capture time. Capture and curation are deliberately separate: interrupting the capture moment to organize defeats the purpose, so the inbox must tolerate mess and the processing pass must be scheduled

title: Knowledge Curation
description: Deliberate selection, organization, and maintenance of knowledge items so they stay useful over time
body_head: # Knowledge Curation  ## Summary Knowledge curation is the active practice of selecting, structuring, and pruning knowledge items so the collection stays findable, trustworthy, and connected. It is the human-or-agent counterpart to search: no retriever can fix a corpus that is messy. mykb's capture-to-synthesis loop is a curation pipeline, not just a storage layer.  ## Details - **Capture vs curate** — capture is cheap (drop everything into an inbox); curation is expensive and continuous (dedupe, re-title, link, retire). - **Operations** — triage, summarize, tag, link, merge duplicates, demote stale items, and promote syntheses from raw notes. - **Worked example** — a weekly mykb review: e

title: Knowledge Integration
description: Weaving separate ideas into coherent, connected understanding
body_head: # Knowledge Integration  ## Summary  Knowledge Integration — Weaving separate ideas into coherent, connected understanding.  ## Details  - Knowledge integration is the process of linking separate facts and ideas into a coherent web — connecting new information to prior knowledge, resolving conflicts between sources, and organizing parts under principles. Linn's knowledge-integration framework studies how learners' fragmented ideas coalesce with instruction. - Mechanisms: eliciting existing ideas, adding new normative ideas, and prompting comparison and reconciliation. Integration predicts transfer: integrated knowledge is flexible, while fragmented facts stay inert. - Worked example: a lea

title: Knowledge Map Research
description: Evidence on maps of knowledge: concept maps, mind maps, and argument maps
body_head: # Knowledge Map Research  ## Summary  Knowledge Map Research — Evidence on maps of knowledge: concept maps, mind maps, and argument maps. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Knowledge maps externalize structure: concepts, relations, and arguments. - Effect sizes vary by task; maps help when they require active construction and use. - Digital knowledge graphs inherit many of the same promises and pitfalls. - mykb's wiki graph is a knowledge map; its edges matter as much as its nodes.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/concept-map-research|Concept Map Research]] — specific form - [[wiki/memory/mind-mapping|Mind Mapping]] —

title: Knowledge Representation
description: Formal schemes — logic, graphs, frames, vectors — for encoding knowledge in systems
body_head: # Knowledge Representation  ## Summary  Knowledge Representation — Formal schemes — logic, graphs, frames, vectors — for encoding knowledge in systems.  ## Details  - Knowledge representation (KR) is the field of encoding knowledge so a system can reason with it. Major schemes include logical formulas, semantic networks and graphs, frames and slots, production rules, and distributed vector embeddings; each trades expressiveness against computational cost and learnability. - Key desiderata (Davis, Shrobe & Szolovits): a representation must stand for the world, support inference, be efficient, and be acquirable. Ontologies supply the vocabulary; knowledge graphs supply the instances. - Worke

title: Leitner System
description: Box-based spaced repetition using error-driven movement between review boxes
body_head: # Leitner System  ## Summary The Leitner system is the simplest family of spaced-repetition schedules: cards live in a series of boxes, a correct answer promotes a card to the next box, and a wrong answer demotes it back to box one. Because each box is reviewed at a longer interval, the system automatically makes difficult cards appear more often and easy cards less often — scheduling by outcome with almost no machinery.  ## Details - **Mechanics** — cards live in boxes; a correct answer promotes a card up, a wrong answer demotes it to box one. Each box is reviewed at a different interval — box one daily, box two every other day, box three weekly, and so on — giving a simple error-driven s

title: Literate Programming
description: Weaving executable code and prose explanations into a single document
body_head: # Literate Programming  ## Summary  Literate Programming — Weaving executable code and prose explanations into a single document. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Knuth's idea: programs are written for humans first, with code blocks woven into explanation. - Tools: Jupyter notebooks, Org-mode babel, and literate Haskell. - Promotes articulation and reproducibility at the cost of toolchain complexity. - A model for knowledge artifacts that mix reasoning, code, and results.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/documentation-practices|Documentation Practices]] — documentation family - [[wiki/memory/knowledge-articulation|Kn

title: Logseq
description: Outliner-based, local-first note app with block-level links and a graph view
body_head: # Logseq  ## Summary Logseq is a local-first knowledge app organized as an outliner, where every block can be linked, tagged, and referenced. Its block-level granularity suits dense interlinking and daily-journal workflows: a single bullet is a first-class addressable unit, so a note can embed another note's bullet instead of copying it.  ## Details - **Blocks** — every bullet is addressable; a block can appear in many places via block references, reducing duplication. A block reference keeps one canonical copy and renders it wherever needed, which is the outliner answer to the copy-paste problem that file-based wikis solve with wikilinks. - **Workflow** — journal-first capture with pages

title: Long-Term Memory Architecture
description: How durable knowledge is organized into declarative and nondeclarative systems
body_head: # Long-Term Memory Architecture  ## Summary  Long-Term Memory Architecture — How durable knowledge is organized into declarative and nondeclarative systems.  ## Details  - Long-term memory is the durable store whose contents survive minutes to decades. Its broadest split is declarative (explicit, verbalizable) versus nondeclarative (implicit, expressed through performance). - Declarative memory divides into episodic (personal events with time and place) and semantic (general facts). Nondeclarative covers procedural skills, priming, conditioning, and habit learning. The hippocampus supports declarative encoding; the neocortex stores the traces; the striatum and cerebellum support procedural

title: Matrix Notes
description: Note-taking in a table with topics as rows and aspects as columns
body_head: # Matrix Notes  ## Summary  Matrix Notes — Note-taking in a table with topics as rows and aspects as columns. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Matrix structure forces comparison across items, prompting relational processing. - Useful for lectures or sources with repeated dimensions (theories × criteria). - Tables become review aids and raw material for concept maps. - Trade-off: rigid columns can distort material that does not fit the grid.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/note-taking-research|Note-Taking Research]] — evidence context - [[wiki/memory/outline-notes|Outline Notes]] — alternative structure - [[wiki/memo

title: Memory and Identity
description: How autobiographical memory constitutes the sense of a continuous self
body_head: # Memory and Identity  ## Summary  Memory and Identity — How autobiographical memory constitutes the sense of a continuous self. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Personal identity depends on being able to narrate a coherent life story. - Amnesia disrupts identity when episodic continuity is lost, even if traits remain. - Memory selection (what we keep and tell) actively shapes who we are. - Relates to narrative identity and autobiographical reasoning.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/narrative-identity|Narrative Identity]] — the storied self - [[wiki/memory/autobiographical-memory|Autobiographical Memory]] — the raw

title: Memory Consolidation
description: Process by which fragile new memories are stabilized and integrated into long-term knowledge
body_head: # Memory Consolidation  ## Summary Memory consolidation is the biological and cognitive process that stabilizes new memories and integrates them with existing knowledge, often during rest and sleep. System consolidation moves memories from hippocampus to cortex over time; synaptic consolidation happens within hours. The metaphor extends directly to knowledge bases: fresh notes need linking and rest before they become durable knowledge.  ## Details - **Synaptic consolidation** — within minutes to hours, protein synthesis stabilizes the synaptic changes encoding a new memory. - **System consolidation** — over days to years, memories are reorganized and integrated into neocortical networks; s

title: Memory Organisation
description: Structures and conventions that arrange memories so they can be found and reused
body_head: # Memory Organisation  ## Summary Memory organisation is how a knowledge base arranges its contents — namespaces, types, indexes, links, and retrieval aids — so items are findable when needed. It is the bridge between storing something and being able to use it: a fact that cannot be found is indistinguishable from a fact that was never stored.  ## Details - **Layers** — physical (directories/files), logical (types, taxonomies), and associative (links, co-occurrence). A well-organized memory works at all three levels at once: the file lives in a predictable place, its frontmatter declares what kind of thing it is, and its links embed it in a web of related items. - **Patterns** — typed name

title: Memory Palace
description: Method of loci: placing to-be-remembered items along a familiar spatial route
body_head: # Memory Palace  ## Summary The memory palace — the method of loci — places to-be-remembered items as vivid images at distinct stations along a familiar spatial route, then recalls them by mentally walking the route and "seeing" what was left at each station. It exploits the robustness of spatial memory to impose an ordered scaffold on arbitrary material, and it is one of the oldest and best-documented mnemonic techniques.  ## Details - **Mechanics** — walk a familiar location mentally, placing vivid images of each item at distinct stations; recall by taking the same route and seeing what was placed at each station. The route provides the order (the sequence of stations) and the retrieval

title: Memory Retrieval Curves
description: Curves describing how recall probability decays with time since last review
body_head: # Memory Retrieval Curves  ## Summary Memory retrieval curves — forgetting curves — show recall probability falling steeply after learning, then more slowly with each successful review. They are the empirical basis for spaced-repetition scheduling and for deciding when an agent should re-surface old knowledge: the curve tells you the right moment to review before recall collapses.  ## Details - **Ebbinghaus curve** — retention decays roughly exponentially without review; the rate varies with material difficulty and prior strength. The steep initial drop is why one session of study produces so little durable memory, and why the first review must come soon after learning. - **Review effect**

title: Memory Schema Effects
description: How prior knowledge structures bias what is encoded and recalled
body_head: # Memory Schema Effects  ## Summary  Memory Schema Effects — How prior knowledge structures bias what is encoded and recalled. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Schemas fill in missing details, aiding gist recall but causing schema-consistent distortions. - Bartlett's classic war-of-the-ghosts work showed systematic transformation toward familiar schemas. - Schema-congruent material is recalled better; incongruent salient items can stand out. - Links to false-memory formation and to top-down processing.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/schema-theory|Schema Theory]] — theoretical basis - [[wiki/memory/false-memory-form

title: Memory Updating
description: Revising stored memories when new evidence arrives
body_head: # Memory Updating  ## Summary  Memory Updating — Revising stored memories when new evidence arrives. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Working-memory updating is the online refresh of current contents; episodic updating revises stored episodes. - Reconsolidation provides a cellular route for targeted revision. - Healthy systems balance stability (keep true memories) and plasticity (correct stale ones). - mykb relevance: knowledge bases face the same stability-plasticity tension as memories.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/reconsolidation|Reconsolidation]] — mechanism for revision - [[wiki/memory/belief-updating|Belie

title: Mental Models
description: Internal working representations of how things work, used for reasoning and prediction
body_head: # Mental Models  ## Summary  Mental Models — Internal working representations of how things work, used for reasoning and prediction.  ## Details  - Mental models are internal representations of systems, situations, or mechanisms that support explanation, prediction, and control. Johnson-Laird's account treats reasoning as model construction and manipulation: people reason by building models of possibilities and testing conclusions against them. - Models are qualitative, incomplete, and often causal — a mechanic's model of an engine, a scientist's model of a reaction, a user's model of an interface. Correct models support transfer; wrong models produce systematic, predictable errors. - Work

title: Mental Time Travel
description: Projecting consciousness into the past and future using episodic memory
body_head: # Mental Time Travel  ## Summary  Mental Time Travel — Projecting consciousness into the past and future using episodic memory. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Tulving's term for the capacity to re-experience the past and pre-experience the future. - Shared neural substrates support remembering and imagining — the constructive-episodic-simulation view. - Distinguishes episodic memory from mere semantic knowledge. - Foundation for planning and for episodic-future-thinking research.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/episodic-future-thinking|Episodic Future Thinking]] — future direction - [[wiki/memory/constructive-epis

title: Metacognition and Monitoring
description: Knowledge and regulation of one's own cognitive processes
body_head: # Metacognition and Monitoring  ## Summary  Metacognition and Monitoring — Knowledge and regulation of one's own cognitive processes.  ## Details  - Metacognition has two faces: knowledge about cognition (knowing how memory, attention, and learning work) and regulation of cognition (planning, monitoring, and evaluating one's performance). Monitoring judgments — feeling-of-knowing, judgments of learning, confidence — steer study decisions. - A well-known failure is calibration: people overestimate what they know (Dunning-Kruger-style effects), and fluency during study is a misleading cue. Delayed self-tests and feedback improve judgment accuracy. - Worked example: after studying, rate how w

title: Method of Loci
description: Memory technique of placing items along a familiar spatial route
body_head: # Method of Loci  ## Summary  Method of Loci — Memory technique of placing items along a familiar spatial route.  ## Details  - The method of loci, or memory palace, encodes items by placing vivid images of them at distinct stations along a familiar route — your home's rooms, a walk to work, a building's floor plan. Recall is a mental walk: each station's image cues its item, and the fixed order of the route provides serial order for free. - Evidence: robust gains in serial recall and list learning, demonstrated in lab studies and by world-record memory athletes; neuroimaging shows the technique recruits spatial and imagery networks. - Worked example: to memorize a shopping list of eight i

title: Mind Mapping
description: Radial diagram that organizes ideas around a central topic with branching associations
body_head: # Mind Mapping  ## Summary Mind mapping draws a central idea with branching topics and sub-topics radiating outward, capturing associations the way a brainstorm produces them. It excels at overview and divergence — seeing the whole shape of a topic fast — and less at precise citation or cross-cutting connections, which is where labeled graphs take over.  ## Details - **Shape** — center = theme; primary branches = major aspects; secondary branches = details; colors and images aid recall. The radial layout keeps everything on one page, which is why maps work well for planning, lectures, and meeting notes where the hierarchy is clear but the details are still forming. - **Strength** — fast, v

title: Misinformation Effect
description: Post-event information altering or implanting memory of the event
body_head: # Misinformation Effect  ## Summary  Misinformation Effect — Post-event information altering or implanting memory of the event.  ## Details  - The misinformation effect is the finding that exposure to misleading post-event information changes what people remember about the original event. Loftus's classic paradigm: witnesses watch an event, then receive a narrative containing a misleading detail (a 'yield' sign instead of 'stop'), and later misreport the original detail. - Mechanisms: source confusion (post-event information misattributed to the event), updating of the original trace, and schema-driven reconstruction. The effect is strongest with plausible misinformation, delay, and repeat

title: Mnemonic Techniques
description: Structured memory aids that add meaning, imagery, or order to material
body_head: # Mnemonic Techniques  ## Summary  Mnemonic Techniques — Structured memory aids that add meaning, imagery, or order to material.  ## Details  - Mnemonic techniques are deliberate encoding strategies that make material more memorable — imagery, rhymes, structure, or meaning. Families include the method of loci (spatial routes), peg systems (number-word images), keyword method (sound-similar imagery), acronyms and acrostics, and narrative methods. - Research support: mnemonics reliably improve recall of lists, vocabulary, names, and ordered material, with effects largest when the material is arbitrary and imageable; they add little to conceptual understanding unless the content itself is mea

title: Mnemonics Research
description: Evidence base for memory aids that elaborate, organize, or peg information
body_head: # Mnemonics Research  ## Summary Mnemonics research is the evidence base for memory aids that elaborate, organize, or peg information: methods like the keyword method, method of loci, peg words, and chunking. The consistent finding across decades of studies is that mnemonic techniques substantially improve recall of serial and list material, with the gains strongest for arbitrary associations and weakest for conceptual understanding.  ## Details - **Evidence base** — mnemonic techniques improve recall by adding structure, imagery, or meaning to otherwise arbitrary material. The keyword method and method of loci show robust gains in paired-associate learning studies: learners using imagery-

title: Model-Based Cognition
description: Thinking and planning that uses internal models of the environment
body_head: # Model-Based Cognition  ## Summary Model-based cognition is thinking that relies on internal models — simulations of how the world works — to predict, plan, and decide. It enables flexibility and counterfactual reasoning at a computational cost. It spans motor control, decisions, and social cognition.  ## Details - **Contrast** — model-free habits use cached values. - **Examples** — mental simulation, planning, imagination. - **In mykb** — models make knowledge usable for prediction.  ## Related - [[wiki/memory/generative-models|Generative Models]] — the machinery - [[wiki/memory/internal-models|Internal Models]] — the stored representations - [[wiki/meta-learning/model-based-learning|Mod

title: Mood-Congruent Memory
description: Tendency to recall material whose emotional tone matches current mood
body_head: # Mood-Congruent Memory  ## Summary  Mood-Congruent Memory — Tendency to recall material whose emotional tone matches current mood. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - People retrieve more positive memories when happy, more negative when sad. - Effect appears in encoding (mood biases attention) and retrieval (mood biases access). - Clinical relevance: depressed mood maintains itself partly through easier access to negative memories. - Pairs with flashbulb-memory as an emotion-memory phenomenon.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/emotional-regulation|Emotional Regulation]] — mood management link - [[wiki/memory/flashbulb-m

title: Motor Learning
description: Acquisition and refinement of movement skills through practice and feedback
body_head: # Motor Learning  ## Summary Motor learning is the process of acquiring movement skills — from typing to sports — through practice, feedback, and consolidation. It progresses from slow, deliberate control to fast, automatic execution. Principles like spacing, variability, and augmented feedback transfer to all skill learning.  ## Details - **Stages** — cognitive, associative, autonomous. - **Key principles** — practice distribution and feedback schedules. - **In mykb** — skill notes capture drills and error patterns.  ## Related - [[wiki/meta-learning/skill-acquisition-stages|Skill Acquisition Stages]] — the phases - [[wiki/memory/forward-models|Forward Models]] — the prediction machinery

title: Music-Cued Memory
description: Songs evoking strong autobiographical and emotional recall
body_head: # Music-Cued Memory  ## Summary  Music functions as one of the most powerful autobiographical cues, reliably retrieving specific life episodes along with the emotions bound to them. Because songs are usually tied to particular periods, places, or people, hearing a familiar tune can bring back vivid details that other cues miss. This matters both for understanding how memory works and for practical applications such as reminiscence therapy, where music restores access to personal memories that otherwise seem lost.  ## Details  - **Cue potency** — music engages several encoding routes at once, pairing auditory features with the personal context in which a song was first heard, which strength

title: Narrative Identity
description: Identity constructed through the internalized life story
body_head: # Narrative Identity  ## Summary  Narrative Identity — Identity constructed through the internalized life story. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - McAdams: people make meaning by integrating life episodes into a coherent narrative. - Narrative identity develops in adolescence and is revised across the lifespan. - Culture supplies story templates that shape which memories are told and how. - mykb relevance: long-running agent projects also benefit from a maintained self-narrative.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/memory-and-identity|Memory and Identity]] — self-memory link - [[wiki/memory/autobiographical-reasoning|Aut

title: Note-Taking Methods
description: Family of structured practices for capturing information during learning and work
body_head: # Note-Taking Methods  ## Summary Note-taking methods are the structured practices used to capture information so it can be reviewed, connected, and reused later. Their choice shapes how well knowledge survives the move from page to memory — the format determines whether the note is reviewable, linkable, and retrievable, or just a faithful record of what was said.  ## Details - **Major families** — outline (linear hierarchy), visual (mind maps, Cornell layouts), and networked (atomic notes with links, Zettelkasten). Each family optimizes for a different outcome: outlines for structure, visual methods for overview, networked methods for reuse. - **Fit matters** — lectures favor Cornell's cu

title: Note-Taking Research
description: Evidence on how note-taking affects encoding, storage, and review
body_head: # Note-Taking Research  ## Summary  Note-Taking Research — Evidence on how note-taking affects encoding, storage, and review. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Notes help learning through encoding (organizing during class) and external storage (review later). - Generative formats outperform verbatim transcription for conceptual learning. - Handwritten vs typed trade-offs are studied under distraction and verbatim-copy accounts. - Findings inform tools from Cornell notes to matrix notes to digital gardens.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/handwritten-vs-typed-notes|Handwritten vs Typed Notes]] — a key comparison - [[wi

title: Number Shape System
description: Mnemonic mapping digits to visual shapes for remembering numbers
body_head: # Number Shape System  ## Summary  Number Shape System — Mnemonic mapping digits to visual shapes for remembering numbers. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Each digit 0-9 maps to an object its shape resembles (e.g., 1 = candle). - Numbers become image sequences that can be placed in a memory palace. - Pairs naturally with the peg system for longer numeric strings. - Good for PINs, phone numbers, and dates.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/peg-system|Peg System]] — ordered peg variant - [[wiki/memory/memory-palace|Memory Palace]] — where images get placed - [[wiki/memory/mnemonic-techniques|Mnemonic Techniques]] — fam

title: Obsidian
description: Local-first markdown note app whose linking, backlinks, and graph views suit networked notes
body_head: # Obsidian  ## Summary Obsidian is a local-first markdown note-taking app built around `wikilinks`, a backlink panel, and a graph view. It popularized the linked-notes workflow that Zettelkasten methods need, with plain files that stay portable — the vault is just a folder of markdown, so no proprietary format stands between the user and their knowledge.  ## Details - **Core** — files are plain markdown on disk; links, backlinks, and graph views derive from the text itself. A `[[wikilink]]` is text in the file, so the graph is a computed view of the files, not a stored structure — which means any tool that reads markdown can participate in the same vault. - **Ecosystem** — plugins add spac

title: Odor-Cued Memory
description: Scents acting as powerful cues for autobiographical recall
body_head: # Odor-Cued Memory  ## Summary  Odor-cued memory refers to the striking ability of scents to trigger vivid autobiographical recollections, often with strong emotional tone. Odors are processed through pathways closely tied to emotion and memory systems, which makes them unusually effective retrieval cues. Understanding this phenomenon matters for memory theory and for applications in reminiscence therapy, marketing, and everyday experience.  ## Details  - **Phenomenon** — a single smell, such as baking bread or a specific perfume, can suddenly bring back a detailed episode from years earlier. - **Anatomical route** — olfactory signals project directly to limbic and memory-related regions,

title: Ontology Design Principles
description: Guidelines for building clean, usable concept and relation vocabularies
body_head: # Ontology Design Principles  ## Summary  Ontology Design Principles — Guidelines for building clean, usable concept and relation vocabularies.  ## Details  - An ontology is an explicit specification of a conceptualization: classes, properties, relations, and constraints. Design principles cluster around clarity (unambiguous names and definitions), coherence (logical consistency), extensibility (new concepts fit without rework), and minimal encoding bias (form follows content, not the tool). - Practical guidance from ontology engineering: reuse existing vocabularies, prefer composition over subclass explosion, keep is-a hierarchies strict, document every class, and test with competency que

title: Ontology Design
description: Modeling a domain's concepts, types, and relations into a formal, shareable schema
body_head: # Ontology Design  ## Summary Ontology design defines the vocabulary of a domain: its classes, properties, and constraints. A well-designed ontology lets different systems share meaning, while an over-engineered one collapses under its own weight. Knowledge graphs need some ontology to be queryable, and mykb's typed wiki (concepts, sources, syntheses) is a lightweight ontology in practice.  ## Details - **Components** — classes (types), properties (relations and attributes), individuals (instances), and axioms (constraints such as disjointness). - **Design trade-off** — top-down ontologies (formal, reusable, slow to build) vs bottom-up folksonomies (cheap, messy); most practical systems si

title: Org Mode
