description: Emacs plain-text outlining and note system with agenda, links, and literate programming
body_head: # Org Mode  ## Summary Org Mode is Emacs' plain-text system for notes, outlines, todos, and agendas, where structure comes from `*` headings in ordinary files. Its longevity and programmability make it the benchmark for text-based personal knowledge tools: an org file from 2005 still opens, edits, and exports today.  ## Details - **Features** — hierarchical outlines, TODO states, timestamps and agendas, inline links, and export to many formats. The agenda turns scattered timestamps and TODOs into a synthesized daily view, and property drawers add structured metadata without leaving plain text. - **Plain text** — everything is editable and greppable; org files survive decades and migrate be

title: Outline Notes
description: Hierarchical indented note-taking that mirrors source structure
body_head: # Outline Notes  ## Summary  Outline Notes — Hierarchical indented note-taking that mirrors source structure. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Hierarchy preserves the source's organization and makes review scanning fast. - Risk: passive copying without transformation, which weakens encoding. - Effective outlines add own-words summaries and questions at each level. - The default structure behind many digital note tools.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/note-taking-research|Note-Taking Research]] — evidence context - [[wiki/memory/matrix-notes|Matrix Notes]] — tabular alternative - [[wiki/memory/handwritten-vs-typed-no

title: PARA Method
description: Organization system that files notes into Projects, Areas, Resources, and Archives
body_head: # PARA Method  ## Summary PARA files everything into four top-level buckets — Projects, Areas, Resources, and Archives — based on the actionability of each item. It is designed to keep knowledge near the work that uses it, so the organization follows what the knowledge is for, not what the knowledge is about.  ## Details - **Buckets** — Projects (active, time-bound), Areas (ongoing responsibilities), Resources (topical references), Archives (inactive everything). A project has a goal and a deadline; an area is a standing responsibility (health, a service you maintain); resources are interests and references; archives hold everything no longer active. - **Principle** — organize by actionabi

title: Peg System
description: Mnemonic that attaches list items to fixed number-word pegs
body_head: # Peg System  ## Summary The peg system is a mnemonic that attaches list items to fixed number-word pegs: each number maps to a memorable word, and the learner visualizes each to-be-remembered item interacting with its peg's image. Because the pegs are fixed and ordered, retrieval is fast — the peg order supplies the list order without any additional mnemonic effort.  ## Details - **Mechanics** — each number 1-10 (or more) maps to a rhyming or shape-based peg word; one classic English set is one-bun, two-shoe, three-tree, four-door, five-hive, six-sticks, seven-heaven, eight-gate, nine-wine, ten-hen. To memorize a list, visualize each item interacting with its peg image — for the third ite

title: Perception as Inference
description: Helmholtzian view that perception is unconscious inference from cues and priors
body_head: # Perception as Inference  ## Summary Perception as inference holds that the brain infers the world from ambiguous cues using prior knowledge — perception is a hypothesis, not a photograph. Illusions reveal the inferences. The view underpins modern Bayesian and predictive accounts of perception.  ## Details - **Helmholtz** — unconscious inference from sensation to object. - **Evidence** — illusions and context effects show inference. - **In mykb** — record observations as hypotheses with confidence.  ## Related - [[wiki/memory/bayesian-brain|Bayesian Brain]] — the modern form - [[wiki/memory/predictive-processing|Predictive Processing]] — the mechanism - [[wiki/memory/top-down-processing|T

title: Personal Knowledge Management
description: Practice of capturing, organizing, and retrieving one's own knowledge for reuse
body_head: # Personal Knowledge Management  ## Summary Personal knowledge management (PKM) is the deliberate system a person uses to capture, connect, and retrieve what they learn. It spans tools, methods, and habits — from paper index cards to AI-assisted wikis like mykb — and its core loop is capture, organize, retrieve, create, repeated until the system becomes part of how the person thinks.  ## Details - **Loop** — capture → organize → retrieve → create; tools serve whichever step is weakest. Most PKM failures are loop failures: capture that never gets organized, organization that never gets retrieved, or retrieval that never feeds creation. - **Methods** — Zettelkasten, PARA, progressive summari

title: Posttraumatic Growth
description: Positive psychological change reported after struggling with adversity
body_head: # Posttraumatic Growth  ## Summary  Posttraumatic Growth — Positive psychological change reported after struggling with adversity. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Growth domains: appreciation of life, relationships, new possibilities, personal strength, spirituality. - Growth and distress can coexist; reporting growth does not mean absence of suffering. - Self-reports may be inflated by retrospective bias and coping narratives. - Related to autobiographical reasoning and meaning-making.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/resilience-research|Resilience Research]] — adaptation sibling - [[wiki/memory/autobiographical-re

title: Precision Weighting
description: Gaining prediction errors by their reliability when updating beliefs
body_head: # Precision Weighting  ## Summary Precision weighting scales prediction errors by their reliability: reliable signals drive large updates, noisy ones small updates. It connects attention to belief updating — attention increases precision. It is central to predictive-coding accounts of attention and to Bayesian models.  ## Details - **Mechanism** — error gain depends on estimated noise. - **Attention link** — attention modulates precision. - **In mykb** — weight evidence by source reliability.  ## Related - [[wiki/memory/predictive-coding|Predictive Coding]] — the framework - [[wiki/memory/bayesian-brain|Bayesian Brain]] — the probability view - [[wiki/memory/attention-and-cognition|Attenti

title: Predictive Coding
description: Computational account of perception as hierarchical prediction-error correction
body_head: # Predictive Coding  ## Summary Predictive coding is the computational theory that cortical areas predict their inputs, send predictions downward, and update with the error signals that flow upward. It explains surround suppression, repetition suppression, and illusion phenomena. It is the leading mechanistic implementation of predictive processing.  ## Details - **Architecture** — prediction units and error units in hierarchies. - **Evidence** — neural responses track prediction errors. - **In mykb** — frame anomalies as prediction errors to investigate.  ## Related - [[wiki/memory/predictive-processing|Predictive Processing]] — the framework - [[wiki/memory/precision-weighting|Precision

title: Predictive Processing
description: Framework where the brain minimizes prediction error by generating and revising models
body_head: # Predictive Processing  ## Summary Predictive processing describes the brain as a prediction machine that constantly anticipates input and updates models when predictions fail. Perception, action, and learning all run on prediction error minimization. It unifies perception, cognition, and motor control under one principle.  ## Details - **Mechanism** — hierarchical prediction and error correction. - **Scope** — perception, action selection, and learning. - **In mykb** — treat surprises as model-update signals.  ## Related - [[wiki/memory/predictive-coding|Predictive Coding]] — the computational version - [[wiki/memory/bayesian-brain|Bayesian Brain]] — the probability framing - [[wiki/ques

title: Prior Knowledge Activation
description: Bringing existing knowledge to bear before and during new learning
body_head: # Prior Knowledge Activation  ## Summary  Prior Knowledge Activation — Bringing existing knowledge to bear before and during new learning.  ## Details  - Prior knowledge is the strongest single predictor of new learning: what you already know determines what you can encode, chunk, and connect. Activation — deliberately retrieving and structuring relevant prior knowledge before study — improves comprehension, elaboration, and retention. - Mechanisms: activated knowledge provides schema slots for new facts, enables elaborative interrogation, and guides attention to what matters. But prior knowledge cuts both ways: wrong or biased priors can distort encoding and resist correction. - Worked ex

title: Proactive Interference
description: Older memories impair retrieval of newer, similar material
body_head: # Proactive Interference  ## Summary  Proactive Interference — Older memories impair retrieval of newer, similar material. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Classic paradigm: learning list A impairs later recall of list B when items overlap. - Explains why learning similar topics back-to-back is harder than interleaving distinct ones. - Release from proactive interference occurs when material changes category. - Motivates interleaved-practice and spaced review.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/interference-theory|Interference Theory]] — parent theory - [[wiki/memory/interleaved-practice|Interleaved Practice]] — counte

title: Progressive Summarization
description: Layering increasingly compressed summaries on a note so its essence surfaces at each revisit
body_head: # Progressive Summarization  ## Summary Progressive summarization adds layers of emphasis to a note over time — bold the best lines, then highlight the best of the bold, then write a one-line summary. Each pass makes the note faster to scan and easier to resurface in future contexts, and because the layers are added only when the note proves useful, effort is never spent compressing notes that do not matter.  ## Details - **Layers** — raw text → bold key passages → highlight the best → executive summary; stop when the note serves its purpose. Layer one is capture (the raw source), layer two is the first curation pass (what mattered when you read it), layer three narrows to the load-bearing

title: Prospective Memory
description: Remembering to perform intended actions in the future
body_head: # Prospective Memory  ## Summary  Prospective Memory — Remembering to perform intended actions in the future.  ## Details  - Prospective memory is remembering to do something later — take the medication, send the email, attend the meeting. It contrasts with retrospective memory (remembering the past) and is notoriously fragile: intentions are easy to form and easy to forget when the moment arrives. - Key distinction: event-based tasks (cue triggers the action — post the letter when you pass the mailbox) versus time-based tasks (act at a time — call at 3pm). Event-based tasks fail when cues are subtle; time-based tasks demand monitoring. - Worked example: you intend to reply to an email; ho

title: Provenance
description: Recorded origin and chain of custody for knowledge items, enabling trust and auditability
body_head: # Provenance  ## Summary Provenance answers 'where did this come from and how did it get here?' — the source URL, capture time, transformation steps, and authorship of a knowledge item. It is what lets an agent trust or discard a claim and what makes knowledge bases auditable. W3C PROV standardizes such records, and mykb's `source:` fields are a lightweight version.  ## Details - **What to record** — origin URL, retrieved-at timestamp, extractor/author, transformations applied, and links to related items. - **Why it matters** — LLM-written wikis otherwise drift into confident fabrication; provenance lets readers and agents trace every claim to evidence. - **Worked example** — a mykb page s

title: Reconsolidation
description: Retrieved memories becoming labile and needing restabilization
body_head: # Reconsolidation  ## Summary  Reconsolidation — Retrieved memories becoming labile and needing restabilization. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - When a memory is reactivated, it enters a brief unstable window before being re-stored. - During that window it can be updated, weakened, or strengthened — the basis of memory-updating. - Research uses reminders + pharmacological or behavioral interference to demonstrate the window. - Implications for therapy (fear memory updating) and for belief-updating systems.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/memory-updating|Memory Updating]] — the adaptive function - [[wiki/memory/syst

title: Reinstatement of Context
description: Restoring study context to improve retrieval of learned material
body_head: # Reinstatement of Context  ## Summary  Reinstatement of context is the process of restoring the physical or mental conditions of a learning episode in order to improve retrieval of the material learned there. Because memory encodes context along with content, returning to that context supplies additional retrieval cues. It matters for study strategy, exam performance, and any setting where knowledge must be recalled away from where it was acquired.  ## Details  - **Mechanism** — contextual features present at encoding become part of the memory trace, so re-presenting them at retrieval increases the chance of successful recall. - **Physical reinstatement** — studying again in the same room

title: Reminiscence Bump
description: Disproportionate recall of autobiographical events from adolescence and early adulthood
body_head: # Reminiscence Bump  ## Summary  Reminiscence Bump — Disproportionate recall of autobiographical events from adolescence and early adulthood. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - People over-50 recall more from ages ~10-30 than adjacent decades. - Explanations include identity formation, novelty, and self-schema consolidation during that period. - Observed across cultures, with some shifts for life transitions. - Relates to narrative-identity and memory-and-identity.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/autobiographical-memory|Autobiographical Memory]] — the bump is a feature of it - [[wiki/memory/narrative-identity|Narrativ

title: Representativeness Heuristic
description: Judging probability by similarity to a stereotype or prototype
body_head: # Representativeness Heuristic  ## Summary  Representativeness Heuristic — Judging probability by similarity to a stereotype or prototype.  ## Details  - The representativeness heuristic judges the probability that something belongs to a category by how similar it looks to the category prototype — ignoring base rates, sample size, and reliability of the evidence. Kahneman & Tversky's lawyer-engineer studies showed people predict by resemblance, not by prior odds. - Signature failures: base-rate neglect (ignoring the prior), the conjunction fallacy (Linda is a bank teller and active feminist), insensitivity to sample size, and gambler's-fallacy-like reasoning. - Worked example: told 70% of

title: Resilience Research
description: Why some people adapt well under adversity and how resilience develops
body_head: # Resilience Research  ## Summary  Resilience Research — Why some people adapt well under adversity and how resilience develops. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Resilience is ordinary adaptation, not rare heroism: most children of adversity function well. - Protective factors include relationships, meaning-making, and self-regulation skills. - Interventions can build resilience but effects depend on risk context. - Links to posttraumatic growth and to emotional regulation.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/posttraumatic-growth|Posttraumatic Growth]] — positive-change outcome - [[wiki/memory/emotional-regulation|Emoti

title: Retrieval-Induced Forgetting
description: Retrieving some memories suppressing access to related competing ones
body_head: # Retrieval-Induced Forgetting  ## Summary  Retrieval-Induced Forgetting — Retrieving some memories suppressing access to related competing ones.  ## Details  - Retrieval-induced forgetting (RIF) is the finding that practicing some items from a category impairs recall of the unpracticed related items. Anderson's retrieval-practice paradigm shows inhibition, not decay: the suppressed items recover when tested with different cues, implicating active inhibitory control. - Mechanism: retrieving a target requires suppressing competing memories that would interfere; the suppression persists, making competitors harder to retrieve later. This is adaptive — it sharpens access — but it means retriev

title: Retrieval Practice
description: Actively recalling information to strengthen memory rather than restudying it
body_head: # Retrieval Practice  ## Summary  Retrieval Practice — Actively recalling information to strengthen memory rather than restudying it.  ## Details  - Retrieval practice is the act of pulling information out of memory instead of re-reading it. Decades of research show attempted retrieval produces stronger long-term retention than restudy of equal duration — the testing effect — even when retrieval fails and feedback follows. - Mechanisms: retrieval strengthens the trace, increases future retrievability (retrieval effort), and creates desirable difficulties that improve encoding. Formats include flashcards, closed-book summaries, practice problems, and self-quizzing. - Worked example: reading

title: Retroactive Interference
description: New memories impair retrieval of older, similar material
body_head: # Retroactive Interference  ## Summary  Retroactive Interference — New memories impair retrieval of older, similar material. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Learning list B after list A hurts later recall of list A. - Strongest when the interfering material is similar to the target. - Sleep and consolidation reduce retroactive interference by stabilizing new traces. - A key reason restudy before sleep outperforms cramming into new material.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/interference-theory|Interference Theory]] — parent theory - [[wiki/memory/proactive-interference|Proactive Interference]] — opposite direction -

title: Scene Construction
description: Building rich mental scenes as the basis of remembering and imagining
body_head: # Scene Construction  ## Summary  Scene Construction — Building rich mental scenes as the basis of remembering and imagining. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Hassabis & Maguire: the hippocampus constructs spatially coherent scenes, reused for recall and imagination. - Scene construction explains why amnesics struggle to imagine novel futures, not only recall pasts. - Imagery vividness varies across people and links to episodic detail. - Central to constructive-episodic-simulation accounts of mental time travel.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/constructive-episodic-simulation|Constructive Episodic Simulation]] — the

title: Schema Theory
description: Organized knowledge structures that guide comprehension, memory, and inference
body_head: # Schema Theory  ## Summary  Schema Theory — Organized knowledge structures that guide comprehension, memory, and inference.  ## Details  - Schemas are structured packages of knowledge about objects, events, and situations — what a restaurant is, what a lecture looks like, how a car works. They provide slots with defaults, so comprehension fills in unstated details and memory reconstructs along schema-consistent lines. - Bartlett's early experiments showed recall transforming toward the rememberer's cultural schemas; modern work ties schemas to faster learning (schema-consistent material is acquired more quickly) and to systematic distortions (schema-inconsistent details are lost or normal

title: Schemas and Stereotypes
description: Knowledge structures about groups that shape perception, memory, and judgment
body_head: # Schemas and Stereotypes  ## Summary  Schemas and Stereotypes — Knowledge structures about groups that shape perception, memory, and judgment. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Stereotypes are group schemas: they economize processing but bias inference and recall. - People remember stereotype-consistent information better and explain away inconsistencies. - Activation can be automatic, though outcomes depend on motivation and context. - A caution for source-memory and for fair evaluation in agent systems.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/memory-schema-effects|Memory Schema Effects]] — general mechanism - [[wiki/memor

title: Second Brain Method
description: Building an external knowledge system (capture, organize, distill, express)
body_head: # Second Brain Method  ## Summary  Second Brain Method — Building an external knowledge system (capture, organize, distill, express). This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Fortescue's PARA/Capture-Organize-Distill-Express framing treats notes as an external working memory. - Second brain systems prioritize actionability and project alignment over encyclopedic coverage. - Criticism: tools alone do not create understanding; retrieval practice and review still matter. - mykb is a second brain with provenance and graph tooling added.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/para-method|PARA Method]] — organization scheme - [[wiki/mem

title: Self-Control Research
description: Empirical study of overriding impulses in favor of longer-term goals
body_head: # Self-Control Research  ## Summary  Self-Control Research — Empirical study of overriding impulses in favor of longer-term goals. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Core paradigms: delay of gratification, temptation resistance, and trait self-report scales. - Mischel's marshmallow studies link early delay ability to later outcomes, with strong SES confounds. - Self-control is trainable through habits, implementation intentions, and environment design. - Bridges decision theory, motivation, and behavior change.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/delay-of-gratification|Delay of Gratification]] — flagship paradigm - [[wiki

title: Self-Explanation
description: Explaining material to oneself to build deeper understanding
body_head: # Self-Explanation  ## Summary  Self-Explanation — Explaining material to oneself to build deeper understanding.  ## Details  - Self-explanation is generating explanations of what one is reading or solving — why a step works, what a concept implies, where it connects. Chi's studies found better learners spontaneously self-explain more, and prompting self-explanation improves learning across science, math, and programming. - The mechanism: self-explanation fills gaps, repairs mental models, and forces the integration of new information with prior knowledge; it also exposes misconceptions that further study can fix. - Worked example: after reading a worked math step, explain to yourself why

title: Self-Regulated Learning
description: Learners planning, monitoring, and adapting their own learning processes
body_head: # Self-Regulated Learning  ## Summary  Self-Regulated Learning — Learners planning, monitoring, and adapting their own learning processes.  ## Details  - Self-regulated learning (SRL) is the cycle of forethought (goal setting, planning), performance (strategy use, monitoring), and self-reflection (evaluation, adaptation). Zimmerman's model frames learners as agents who set goals, select strategies, and adjust based on feedback. - Effective SRL predicts achievement beyond ability: learners who plan, self-test, and repair misunderstandings outperform equally able peers who study passively. Strategy training plus metacognitive prompts reliably improves outcomes. - Worked example: before a stu

title: Semantic Networks
description: Graphs of concepts connected by labeled relations, used in cognition and computing
body_head: # Semantic Networks  ## Summary  Semantic Networks — Graphs of concepts connected by labeled relations, used in cognition and computing.  ## Details  - Semantic networks represent knowledge as nodes (concepts) and labeled edges (relations such as is-a, part-of, causes). Collins and Quillian's cognitive model proposed hierarchical storage with cognitive economy — properties stored at the highest applicable node — later revised as spreading-activation theory. - Empirical support: semantic priming (doctor primes nurse), category-size effects, and the fan effect (more links slow verification) shaped both psychology and AI knowledge representation. Modern knowledge graphs operationalize the sam

title: Semantic Prospection
description: Predicting future events from general knowledge rather than episodic simulation
body_head: # Semantic Prospection  ## Summary  Semantic Prospection — Predicting future events from general knowledge rather than episodic simulation. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Not all future thought is episodic; semantic knowledge supports expectations and scripts. - Semantic prospection is faster and less effortful than building novel scenes. - Both routes combine in planning; disruptions dissociate in patient studies. - Complement to episodic-future-thinking and scene construction.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/episodic-future-thinking|Episodic Future Thinking]] — episodic counterpart - [[wiki/concepts/scripts-and-

title: Serial Position Effect
description: Better recall of the first and last items of a list, weaker middle
body_head: # Serial Position Effect  ## Summary  Serial Position Effect — Better recall of the first and last items of a list, weaker middle.  ## Details  - The serial position effect is the U-shaped pattern of recall across a list: primacy (first items recalled best) and recency (last items recalled best) with a dip in the middle. Primacy reflects extra rehearsal and transfer to long-term memory; recency reflects items still in working memory. - The classic dissociation: a delay or distracter task between study and test eliminates recency but not primacy; increasing presentation rate weakens primacy. The effect is foundational evidence for separate short- and long-term stores. - Worked example: afte

title: Situated Cognition
description: Cognition bound to context, activity, and culture rather than abstract rules
body_head: # Situated Cognition  ## Summary  Situated Cognition — Cognition bound to context, activity, and culture rather than abstract rules.  ## Details  - Situated cognition holds that knowing and thinking are inseparable from the contexts and activities in which they occur. Lave's studies of supermarket arithmetic showed shoppers computing accurately in context while failing the same math in abstract form — knowledge is co-produced with its situation. - Implications: learning is most effective in authentic activity (apprenticeship, real problems), and abstract knowledge often stays inert when separated from use. Critics note the difficulty of defining 'situation' and the demonstrated value of so

title: Sketchnoting
description: Live visual note-taking combining text, icons, and layout
body_head: # Sketchnoting  ## Summary  Sketchnoting — Live visual note-taking combining text, icons, and layout. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Sketchnotes blend words and drawings to capture talks and meetings in real time. - Success depends on listening-plus-encoding, not artistic skill. - Layout conveys hierarchy and flow that linear text flattens. - Pairs with visual-note-taking and dual-coding rationale.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/visual-note-taking|Visual Note-Taking]] — umbrella practice - [[wiki/memory/dual-coding-theory|Dual Coding Theory]] — why images help - [[wiki/memory/note-taking-research|Note-Taking Rese

title: Sleep and Memory
description: How sleep consolidates, reorganizes, and protects memories
body_head: # Sleep and Memory  ## Summary  Sleep and Memory — How sleep consolidates, reorganizes, and protects memories.  ## Details  - Sleep is a privileged state for memory: during slow-wave sleep, hippocampal traces are replayed and reorganized into neocortical storage; REM sleep supports emotional and procedural consolidation. Sleep deprivation impairs encoding, consolidation, and retrieval the next day. - Key findings: memories reactivated during sleep (cued by sounds or odors) improve; naps consolidate declarative and motor learning; sleep after learning reduces interference and strengthens gist extraction. The systems-consolidation account places sleep at the center of the transfer from hippo

title: Source Memory
description: Remembering where, when, and from whom information came
body_head: # Source Memory  ## Summary  Source Memory — Remembering where, when, and from whom information came.  ## Details  - Source memory is memory for the origin of information — who said it, where you read it, when it happened — as distinct from memory for the content. Source monitoring is the set of processes that attribute memories to sources (external event, dream, imagination, another person). - Source errors drive many real-world failures: misattributing a friend's suggestion as your own, recalling imagined events as real (reality monitoring failures), and the sleeper effect (forgetting the source of a message while keeping its content). - Worked example: you remember a striking claim but

title: Spaced Memorization
description: Applying spaced-repetition scheduling to deliberate memorization
body_head: # Spaced Memorization  ## Summary  Spaced memorization applies spaced-repetition scheduling to deliberate memorization: selecting material, scheduling reviews, and measuring retention. It converts forgetting from a failure into a plan. It matters because durable memory is built by timing, not by repetition volume. For knowledge systems, the same logic suggests scheduling re-verification of facts, not just human reviews.  ## Details  - **Definition** — Spaced memorization is intentional learning where review is scheduled at expanding intervals to counteract forgetting. - **Contrast with incidental learning** — Unlike passive exposure, spaced memorization selects items, schedules practice, a

title: Spaced Repetition Systems
description: Schedulers that time reviews at expanding intervals to combat forgetting
body_head: # Spaced Repetition Systems  ## Summary  Spaced Repetition Systems — Schedulers that time reviews at expanding intervals to combat forgetting.  ## Details  - Spaced repetition systems (SRS) schedule reviews of individual items at expanding intervals, timing each review just before the item is likely to be forgotten. The family ranges from Leitner boxes to per-item algorithms like SM-2 and FSRS. - SM-2 (SuperMemo's 1987 algorithm) grades each card and multiplies or resets the interval based on quality; Anki popularized it. FSRS is a modern free-spaced-repetition predictor that fits a forgetting model to each learner's history. Leitner boxes offer a simple error-driven version with fixed box

title: Spaced Repetition
description: Learning technique that schedules reviews at expanding intervals to maximize long-term retention
body_head: # Spaced Repetition  ## Summary Spaced repetition schedules reviews of an item just before it would be forgotten, using expanding intervals driven by each answer's difficulty. It exploits the spacing effect and the testing effect to make retention dramatically more efficient than cramming. For agents, the same idea applies to re-reviewing memories so old knowledge stays retrievable.  ## Details - **Mechanism** — each review grades difficulty (again/hard/good/easy); the algorithm grows or shrinks the interval accordingly (SM-2, FSRS, Leitner boxes). - **Spacing effect** — distributed practice beats massed practice for long-term retention; the effect is among the most replicated findings in

title: Spacing Effect
description: Distributed practice producing better retention than massed practice
body_head: # Spacing Effect  ## Summary  Spacing Effect — Distributed practice producing better retention than massed practice.  ## Details  - The spacing effect is the finding that spreading study sessions apart in time produces better long-term retention than massing them together, even when total study time is equal. It is one of the most replicated findings in cognitive psychology, demonstrated across ages, materials, and delays. - Key facts: longer gaps generally help retention but hurt initial performance (the study feels harder); inter-session sleep and consolidation contribute; the effect interacts with retrieval practice to multiply gains. - Worked example: 30 minutes of vocabulary practice

title: State-Dependent Memory
description: Recall influenced by matching internal physiological or emotional states
body_head: # State-Dependent Memory  ## Summary  State-Dependent Memory — Recall influenced by matching internal physiological or emotional states.  ## Details  - State-dependent memory is the analogue of context dependence for internal states: retrieval improves when the learner's internal state at test matches the state at encoding. Demonstrated with mood (happy-learned material recalled better when happy) and with drug states in classic pharmacological studies. - The effect is smaller and more variable than environmental context effects, and it is entangled with mood-congruent processing — mood biases what is encoded and retrieved, not just cueing. - Worked example: material studied while anxious

title: Story Method
description: Mnemonic that weaves list items into a single narrative
body_head: # Story Method  ## Summary  Story Method — Mnemonic that weaves list items into a single narrative. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Items are linked into a coherent story, giving each a role in a remembered sequence. - The narrative provides retrieval order and contextual cues at recall time. - Vivid, unusual imagery makes the story more memorable. - Useful for shopping lists, speeches, and any ordered sequence.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/mnemonic-techniques|Mnemonic Techniques]] — family member - [[wiki/concepts/story-grammar|Story Grammar]] — narrative structure research - [[wiki/memory/mental-time-travel|Me

title: Summarization Cognition
description: Cognitive processes underlying condensing texts into shorter faithful versions
body_head: # Summarization Cognition  ## Summary  Summarization Cognition — Cognitive processes underlying condensing texts into shorter faithful versions. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Summarization recruits selection, deletion, generalization, and transformation of source content. - Quality depends on comprehension and on knowing the audience's prior knowledge. - Research spans discourse processing, reading comprehension, and now LLM summarization. - Useful lens for note-taking and for evaluating AI-generated summaries in mykb.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/gist-extraction|Gist Extraction]] — core meaning operation - [[

title: Synaptic Consolidation
description: Rapid cellular strengthening of memory traces within minutes to hours
body_head: # Synaptic Consolidation  ## Summary  Synaptic Consolidation — Rapid cellular strengthening of memory traces within minutes to hours. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Involves LTP-like changes: receptor trafficking, gene expression, and structural change at synapses. - Completes within hours and is disrupted by protein-synthesis inhibitors. - Distinct from systems consolidation, which reorganizes storage locations over time. - Basis of the claim that early sleep helps fix what was encoded that day.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/systems-consolidation|Systems Consolidation]] — slow, systems-level complement - [[wiki

title: Systems Consolidation
description: Gradual reorganization of memories from hippocampus to neocortex over time
body_head: # Systems Consolidation  ## Summary Systems consolidation is the gradual reorganization of memories over weeks to years, in which traces that initially depend on the hippocampus become supported by the neocortex. The hippocampus acts as a fast temporary index that replays experiences into slow cortical connections; once those connections are strong enough, the memory survives without the hippocampal index.  ## Details - **Mechanics** — new episodic memories depend on the hippocampus and become neocortically supported over weeks to years. The standard theory is that hippocampal replay trains cortical connections until the trace is independent; each replay strengthens the cortical schema whi

title: Taxonomy
description: Hierarchical classification of a domain into ordered categories used for organization and retrieval
body_head: # Taxonomy  ## Summary A taxonomy organizes a domain into a hierarchical tree of categories, from broad classes down to specific items. It gives every item one canonical place, which is great for browsing and governance and limiting for ideas that belong in several places. Wiki systems blend taxonomies (namespaces) with linking to escape that limitation.  ## Details - **Structure** — tree of parent-child categories; items may be leaves or further subdivided; depth and breadth trade browseability against maintenance. - **Where it shines** — file systems, library classification, permissions, and faceted navigation with controlled vocabularies. - **Where it fails** — cross-cutting topics (e.g

title: Testing Effect
description: The finding that retrieving information improves long-term retention more than restudying
body_head: # Testing Effect  ## Summary  Testing Effect — The finding that retrieving information improves long-term retention more than restudying.  ## Details  - The testing effect is the robust finding that taking a test on material improves later retention more than an equal amount of restudy. It holds across age groups, materials, and delay intervals, and it survives deep processing controls: retrieval itself, not just extra exposure, produces the benefit. - Key boundary conditions: feedback improves the effect (correcting errors beats testing alone), effortful retrieval beats easy recognition, and the benefit is largest on delayed tests — the opposite pattern from cramming. - Worked example: tw

title: Tip-of-the-Tongue State
description: Felt near-access to a memory that cannot be fully retrieved
body_head: # Tip-of-the-Tongue State  ## Summary  Tip-of-the-Tongue State — Felt near-access to a memory that cannot be fully retrieved. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Strong feeling of imminent recall with partial access: first letter, syllables, meaning. - Often resolved by retrieval cues, delay, or looking the item up (which fixes it). - Studied as a retrieval failure with intact semantic activation. - Metacognitive angle: the feeling is a judgment about memory access, not the memory itself.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/metacognition-and-monitoring|Metacognition and Monitoring]] — feeling-of-knowing judgments - [[wiki/

title: Top-Down Processing
description: Perception and cognition shaped by expectations, knowledge, and context
body_head: # Top-Down Processing  ## Summary Top-down processing uses knowledge, expectations, and context to interpret sensory input, making perception fast and meaningful — and fallible. It is the counterpart to bottom-up data flow and is prominent in reading, object recognition, and ambiguous stimuli.  ## Details - **Examples** — reading misspelled words, seeing faces in clouds. - **Cost** — illusions and expectation-driven errors. - **In mykb** — label assumptions when interpreting data.  ## Related - [[wiki/memory/bottom-up-processing|Bottom-Up Processing]] — the data-driven counterpart - [[wiki/memory/predictive-processing|Predictive Processing]] — the modern theory - [[wiki/memory/expectancy-e

title: Transactive Memory
description: Shared system where group members specialize in remembering different domains
body_head: # Transactive Memory  ## Summary  Transactive Memory — Shared system where group members specialize in remembering different domains.  ## Details  - Transactive memory is a group-level memory system: members encode, store, and retrieve knowledge in a division of labor, plus a shared directory of who knows what. Wegner's theory explains how couples, teams, and organizations remember more than any member could alone. - The directory is the key structure: knowing who knows makes retrieval a routing problem. Systems form through communication and role differentiation, and they break down when members leave or the directory goes stale. - Worked example: a team where Alice owns the API details,

title: Transfer-Appropriate Processing
description: Memory best when encoding and retrieval processes overlap
body_head: # Transfer-Appropriate Processing  ## Summary  Transfer-Appropriate Processing — Memory best when encoding and retrieval processes overlap. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Morris, Bransford & Franks: depth is not the whole story; what matters is the match between study and test processing. - Implication: practice the format you will need — recognition for recognition, recall for recall, application for application.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/encoding-specificity|Encoding Specificity]] — companion principle - [[wiki/memory/encoding-retrieval-match|Encoding-Retrieval Match]] — the general form - [[wiki/memory/re

title: Transfer of Learning
description: Applying knowledge or skill from one context to another
body_head: # Transfer of Learning  ## Summary  Transfer of Learning — Applying knowledge or skill from one context to another.  ## Details  - Transfer of learning is the use of prior knowledge in new situations. It spans near transfer (same skill, slightly different context) to far transfer (structure applied to a novel domain). Classic experiments — Gick and Holyoak's radiation problem — show that spontaneous far transfer is rare unless the learner abstracts the underlying principle. - Factors that promote transfer: multiple varied examples, practice that tests application rather than recognition, abstract representation of the principle, and learning in contexts that resemble the target. Transfer i

title: Visual Note-Taking
description: Notes that combine drawing, layout, and text to capture and structure ideas
body_head: # Visual Note-Taking  ## Summary  Visual note-taking combines drawing, layout, and text to capture and structure ideas in a single canvas. Instead of recording information as plain linear prose, it uses space, icons, and typography to show relationships at a glance. This matters because the format itself supports comprehension and later recall: images and spatial layout add a second retrieval route alongside the words.  ## Details  - **Definition** — visual notes are rendered documents, often sketched live, where hierarchy, flow, and emphasis are encoded through layout rather than sentence structure. - **Dual-coding rationale** — under dual-coding theory, information stored as both verbal

title: Wiki Science
description: Study of how wikis and collaborative knowledge bases grow, stay coherent, and resist degradation
body_head: # Wiki Science  ## Summary Wiki science examines why some wikis thrive — high link density, stable structure, low duplication — while others decay into chaos. It studies editing norms, graph structure, and the social mechanics that keep knowledge bases coherent. mykb is a single-agent wiki, so the relevant lessons are structural: atomic pages, backlinks, and clear namespaces.  ## Details - **Structural findings** — coherent wikis exhibit power-law link distributions, short paths between pages, and page titles that carry meaning. - **Governance** — clear rules (naming conventions, page ownership, review processes) prevent forking and duplicated content. - **Worked example** — mykb's `wiki/c

title: Willpower Research
description: Scientific study of self-control as a limited or flexible resource
body_head: # Willpower Research  ## Summary  Willpower Research — Scientific study of self-control as a limited or flexible resource. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Baumeister's ego-depletion model treated self-control as a depletable resource; replication attempts have weakened the effect. - Alternative accounts: motivation, glucose beliefs, and task-switching explain apparent depletion. - Trait self-control predicts better life outcomes across health, finance, and relationships. - mykb relevance: willpower claims should be cited with current meta-analytic status.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/self-control-research|Self-C

title: Working Memory Capacity
description: The individual limit on information that can be held and processed at once
body_head: # Working Memory Capacity  ## Summary  Working Memory Capacity — The individual limit on information that can be held and processed at once.  ## Details  - Working memory capacity (WMC) is the amount of information a person can hold and manipulate simultaneously. Miller's 'magical number seven' framed short-term span; modern estimates for working memory proper are around four chunks (Cowan), with substantial individual differences. - Measurement: complex span tasks (remember items while processing — e.g., solve sums while recalling letters) predict reading comprehension, reasoning, and fluid intelligence better than simple span. WMC is partly heritable but trainable within limits, with tra

title: Working Memory Model
description: Baddeley's multicomponent account of the small capacity system that holds and manipulates information online
body_head: # Working Memory Model  ## Summary  Working Memory Model — Baddeley's multicomponent account of the small capacity system that holds and manipulates information online.  ## Details  - Working memory is the limited-capacity workspace for holding and manipulating information during cognition. Baddeley and Hitch's model splits it into a central executive plus three stores: the phonological loop (verbal rehearsal), the visuospatial sketchpad (visual and spatial imagery), and the episodic buffer (binding across modalities and long-term memory). - The central executive controls attention, task switching, and the allocation of the slave systems. Capacity is roughly four chunks; measured by spans,

title: Zettelkasten Method
description: Slip-box note system of atomic notes linked into a web of thought
body_head: # Zettelkasten Method  ## Summary  Zettelkasten Method — Slip-box note system of atomic notes linked into a web of thought. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Luhmann's method: permanent atomic notes, each with a stable ID, linked by relations. - Value comes from the link structure: notes are nodes, writing happens by assembling existing notes.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/zettelkasten|Zettelkasten]] — mykb's existing article - [[wiki/memory/atomic-notes-practice|Atomic Notes Practice]] — the unit of the system - [[wiki/memory/backlinks-research|Backlinks Research]] — graph navigation

title: Zettelkasten
description: Note-taking method built on atomic, linked, permanent notes that grow into a web of thought
body_head: # Zettelkasten  ## Summary Zettelkasten (German for 'slip box') is a method of keeping permanent, atomic notes that are densely linked rather than filed by topic. Ideas emerge from the network instead of from a fixed outline. Modern tools like Obsidian and Logseq implement it digitally, and mykb's wiki is structurally a networked slip box.  ## Details - **Core rules** — one idea per note; write in your own words; link every note to context; number for identity (modern tools use IDs instead). - **Why it works** — links create serendipity: retrieval follows the network, and new notes attach to old ones, compounding over time. - **Worked example** — a note 'spaced repetition beats cramming' l

title: Academic Emotions
description: Emotions experienced in achievement and learning settings
body_head: # Academic Emotions  ## Summary  Academic Emotions — Emotions experienced in achievement and learning settings. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Include enjoyment, hope, pride, anxiety, boredom, shame, and anger. - Control-value theory links appraisals of control and value to specific emotions. - Emotions affect attention, strategy use, and persistence. - Domain-general versus domain-specific patterns differ across subjects.  ## Related  - [[wiki/meta-learning/achievement-emotion-theory|Achievement Emotion Theory]] — explanatory framework - [[wiki/meta-learning/test-anxiety|Test Anxiety]] — flagship case - [[wiki

title: Academic Self-Concept
description: Self-perceptions of ability in academic domains
body_head: # Academic Self-Concept  ## Summary  Academic self-concept is the set of self-perceptions a person holds about their abilities in academic domains, such as mathematics, verbal skills, or specific subjects. It is domain-specific rather than global and is reciprocally related to achievement: performance shapes self-concept, and self-concept shapes subsequent performance. The concept matters because it influences course choice, effort, and persistence throughout education.  ## Details  - **Definition** — academic self-concept is a person's appraisal of their competence in academic content areas, organized hierarchically and by domain. - **Domain specificity** — a student can have high math se

title: Achievement Emotion Theory
description: Pekrun's control-value theory of emotions in achievement settings
body_head: # Achievement Emotion Theory  ## Summary  Achievement emotion theory, chiefly developed by Pekrun, explains the emotions students experience in achievement settings through appraisals of control and value. Pride, anxiety, boredom, enjoyment, and shame are not side effects of learning; they shape attention, motivation, and strategy use. The theory matters because emotions feed back into achievement, making emotional regulation part of effective learning. Emotions are not merely consequences of achievement; they are causes of it, which makes emotional climate an instructional variable.  ## Details  - **Definition** — achievement emotions are emotions tied to achievement activities and outcom

title: Achievement Goal Theory
description: Framework explaining motivation through the goals students pursue in achievement settings
body_head: # Achievement Goal Theory  ## Summary  Achievement goal theory explains motivation in achievement settings through the goals people pursue, principally mastery goals focused on developing competence and performance goals focused on demonstrating it. The framework has grown to include approach and avoidance variants of each goal type. It matters because goals predict how learners approach tasks, interpret feedback, and respond to difficulty, and because classroom structures shape which goals dominate. Goal orientations are not fixed traits; they shift with the situation, so classroom climate is a lever for changing how learners engage.  ## Details  - **Definition** — achievement goals are t

title: Adaptive Learning Systems
description: Systems that tailor content, pacing, and feedback to each learner
body_head: # Adaptive Learning Systems  ## Summary  Adaptive Learning Systems — Systems that tailor content, pacing, and feedback to each learner.  ## Details  - Adaptive learning systems adjust the learning experience in real time — which item, how much support, what difficulty — based on a model of the learner. The engine combines knowledge tracing or IRT with decision policies: select the next item that maximizes information or learning gain. - Evidence: adaptive item selection improves efficiency and outcomes versus fixed sequences in well-measured domains, especially with mastery-based stopping. Benefits shrink when measurement is poor or content is open-ended. - Worked example: a language app t

title: Agentic Engagement
description: Students' proactive, constructive contribution to their own learning environment
body_head: # Agentic Engagement  ## Summary  Agentic Engagement — Students' proactive, constructive contribution to their own learning environment. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Reeve's fourth dimension: students ask questions, express preferences, and shape instruction. - Agentic behavior predicts motivational gains beyond the other engagement dimensions. - Requires autonomy support and psychological safety. - Mirrors self-direction goals in agent systems and RSIS3.  ## Related  - [[wiki/meta-learning/engagement-research|Engagement Research]] — umbrella field - [[wiki/meta-learning/autonomy-support|Autonomy Support]] —

title: Approach-Avoidance Motivation
description: Twin motivational systems: pursuing rewards and avoiding threats
body_head: # Approach-Avoidance Motivation  ## Summary  Approach-avoidance motivation describes two fundamental motivational systems: one oriented toward pursuing rewards and desirable outcomes, the other toward avoiding threats and undesirable outcomes. The balance between these systems shapes emotion, attention, and behavior in achievement and everyday settings. The distinction matters because approach and avoidance are not simply opposites — each has distinct antecedents, physiology, and consequences. The two systems are asymmetrical: losses and threats generally capture attention more strongly than equivalent rewards, which has consequences for how tasks are framed.  ## Details  - **Definition**

title: Athlete Cognition
description: Cognitive processes underlying elite sports performance
body_head: # Athlete Cognition  ## Summary  Athlete Cognition — Cognitive processes underlying elite sports performance. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Includes anticipation, decision-making, and attentional focus under pressure. - Experts read opponents' cues earlier and more accurately. - Quiet-eye and choking studies connect attention to performance. - Training can improve perceptual-cognitive skills in sport.  ## Related  - [[wiki/meta-learning/perceptual-expertise|Perceptual Expertise]] — perception base - [[wiki/memory/attention-and-cognition|Attention and Cognition]] — focus under load - [[wiki/meta-learning/delibe

title: Attribution Theory
description: How people explain causes of events and how explanations shape motivation
body_head: # Attribution Theory  ## Summary  Attribution theory describes how people explain the causes of events and how those explanations shape emotion, motivation, and future behavior. In achievement settings, the key causal dimensions are locus, stability, and controllability. The theory matters because the explanation a learner gives for success or failure — not the outcome itself — often determines whether they persist or give up.  ## Details  - **Definition** — attribution theory studies the perceived causes of outcomes and the consequences of those causal beliefs for affect and action. - **Causal dimensions** — causes are classified by locus (internal or external), stability (stable or fluct

title: Automaticity Research
description: Study of behaviors that become fast, effortless, and attention-free with practice
body_head: # Automaticity Research  ## Summary  Automaticity Research — Study of behaviors that become fast, effortless, and attention-free with practice. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Automatic processes run without intent, effort, or capacity limits. - Stroop interference and skilled typing show automatic components. - Automaticity frees attention for higher-level control. - Develops through extensive consistent practice, per skill-acquisition models.  ## Related  - [[wiki/meta-learning/skill-acquisition-stages|Skill Acquisition Stages]] — development path - [[wiki/meta-learning/proceduralization|Proceduralization]] —

title: Autonomy Support
description: Interpersonal styles that offer choice, rationale, and perspective-taking
body_head: # Autonomy Support  ## Summary  Autonomy support is an interpersonal style in which teachers, parents, coaches, or managers offer choice, provide rationales, and take the learner's perspective instead of controlling behavior. It is a central construct in self-determination theory, where it is distinguished from permissiveness. Autonomy-supportive environments matter because they increase internalized motivation, engagement, and persistence across educational and organizational settings.  ## Details  - **Definition** — autonomy support means acknowledging the other person's frame of reference, offering meaningful options, and explaining why requested actions matter. - **Not permissiveness**

title: Behavioral Engagement
description: Visible participation: attendance, effort, and on-task conduct
body_head: # Behavioral Engagement  ## Summary  Behavioral Engagement — Visible participation: attendance, effort, and on-task conduct. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Measured via attendance, participation, time-on-task, and persistence. - Necessary but not sufficient for deep learning. - First target of interventions; often easiest to observe and log. - In systems, behavioral signals feed learning analytics.  ## Related  - [[wiki/meta-learning/engagement-research|Engagement Research]] — umbrella field - [[wiki/meta-learning/cognitive-engagement|Cognitive Engagement]] — deeper sibling - [[wiki/meta-learning/learning-analy

title: Bi-Encoder
description: Model encoding query and document separately into vectors for fast similarity search
body_head: # Bi-Encoder  ## Summary A bi-encoder runs the query and each document through the same encoder independently, producing vectors that are compared by cosine or dot product. Because document vectors are precomputed, it is the architecture behind scalable semantic search.  ## Details - **Mechanism** — two encoders (often weight-shared) → one vector each → similarity score; nothing is computed per query-document pair, so all document vectors can be embedded once and indexed ahead of time. - **Use** — first-stage retrieval over millions of items; the vectors live in a vector database with approximate nearest-neighbour indexes (HNSW, IVF), so a query scans candidates in milliseconds rather than

title: Boredom Research
description: Study of boredom's causes, correlates, and consequences in learning
body_head: # Boredom Research  ## Summary  Boredom Research — Study of boredom's causes, correlates, and consequences in learning. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Boredom arises from attentional and value failures: task too easy, hard, or meaningless. - In learning it predicts distraction, poorer performance, and disengagement. - Can be functional — signaling that current activity lacks value — or dysfunctional. - Relevant to task design and to academic-emotions research.  ## Related  - [[wiki/meta-learning/academic-emotions|Academic Emotions]] — taxonomy home - [[wiki/meta-learning/cognitive-engagement|Cognitive Engagemen

title: Calibration Training
description: Practice that improves the match between confidence and accuracy
body_head: # Calibration Training  ## Summary  Calibration Training — Practice that improves the match between confidence and accuracy. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Methods: confidence ratings with immediate outcome feedback, bracketing, and review. - Training transfers when feedback is frequent and domains are stable. - Overconfidence is sticky; debiasing must be sustained. - Serves forecasting, self-assessment, and decision quality.  ## Related  - [[wiki/meta-learning/self-assessment-accuracy|Self-Assessment Accuracy]] — what training improves - [[wiki/meta-learning/confidence-ratings|Confidence Ratings]] — measuremen

title: Self-Improvement Cycles

title: Category Learning
description: Acquiring the criteria that group objects, events, or ideas together
body_head: # Category Learning  ## Summary Category learning is the acquisition of groupings — how to tell birds from bats, bugs from features. It proceeds through rules, prototypes, or exemplars depending on the structure and the learner. Categories organize perception, memory, and generalization.  ## Details - **Theories** — prototype, exemplar, and rule-based accounts. - **Development** — children learn categories from labels and similarity. - **Expertise** — experts use finer, more diagnostic categories. - **In mykb** — taxonomy design is category learning made explicit.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/prototype-theory|Prototype Theory]] — averaged representations - [[wiki/concepts/exemplar-theory|

title: Chess Expertise
description: The classic research domain for expert memory and pattern recognition
body_head: # Chess Expertise  ## Summary  Chess Expertise — The classic research domain for expert memory and pattern recognition. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Chase & Simon: masters recall real board positions far better than novices, but random boards no better. - Expertise rests on thousands of stored patterns (chunks). - Calculation and evaluation skills also grow with practice. - De Groot showed masters search fewer, better moves.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/chunking-and-encoding|Chunking and Encoding]] — chunk account - [[wiki/meta-learning/pattern-recognition-expertise|Pattern Recognition Expertise]] — pattern b

title: Choice Architecture

body_head: # Choice Architecture  ## Summary  Choice Architecture — Designing the context in which people make decisions. title: Cluster Analysis
description: Grouping items so similar ones share a cluster, revealing structure without labels
body_head: # Cluster Analysis  ## Summary Cluster analysis partitions a set of items — documents, embeddings, notes — so members of a cluster are more similar to each other than to outsiders. It is the unsupervised workhorse for organization, deduplication, and topic discovery.  ## Details - **Algorithms** — k-means (centroid, fast but assumes spherical clusters and needs k), hierarchical (agglomerative tree, gives a dendrogram and any cut), DBSCAN (density-based, finds arbitrary shapes and noise points), and spectral (graph-based, uses the eigenstructure of a similarity matrix); embeddings make vector clustering universal because any item becomes a fixed-length vector. - **Choosing k** — the eternal

title: Coach Feedback
description: External, expert-provided feedback that guides skill improvement
body_head: # Coach Feedback  ## Summary  Coach Feedback — External, expert-provided feedback that guides skill improvement. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Coaches diagnose errors, prescribe drills, and set challenge levels. - Effective feedback is immediate, specific, and actionable. - Coach presence adds accountability and external perspective. - Central to deliberate practice as Ericsson defines it.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/deliberate-practice|Deliberate Practice]] — why coaches matter - [[wiki/meta-learning/feedforward|Feedforward]] — future-focused form - [[wiki/episodes/after-action-review|After Action Review]] —

title: Cognitive Apprenticeship
description: Teaching by modeling, coaching, and fading expert thinking processes
body_head: # Cognitive Apprenticeship  ## Summary  Cognitive Apprenticeship — Teaching by modeling, coaching, and fading expert thinking processes.  ## Details  - Cognitive apprenticeship makes expert thinking visible: novices learn by watching experts model cognitive work — not just final products — then practicing with coaching while support fades. Collins, Brown & Newman's model imports the apprenticeship form into schooled domains like reading, writing, and math. - Six methods: modeling (expert thinks aloud), coaching (feedback on attempts), scaffolding (support that fades), articulation (learner explains reasoning), reflection (comparing own process to experts'), and exploration (learner sets ow

title: Cognitive Diagnosis Models
description: Models that infer fine-grained knowledge states from response patterns
body_head: # Cognitive Diagnosis Models  ## Summary  Cognitive Diagnosis Models — Models that infer fine-grained knowledge states from response patterns.  ## Details  - Cognitive diagnosis models (CDMs) infer which specific skills or attributes a learner has mastered from their response patterns, rather than estimating a single ability score. The DINA model, for example, assumes a set of attributes, a Q-matrix mapping items to attributes, and a conjunctive rule: mastery of all required attributes is needed to answer correctly. - Output is a profile — mastered, partial, or unmastered per skill — which is more actionable for remediation than a total score. CDMs connect psychometrics to cognitive theory

title: Cognitive Engagement
description: Psychological investment and strategy use in learning tasks
body_head: # Cognitive Engagement  ## Summary  Cognitive Engagement — Psychological investment and strategy use in learning tasks. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Involves self-regulation, deep processing, and willingness to exert mental effort. - Distinct from mere time-on-task; quality of processing matters. - Promoted by autonomy support, challenge, and meaningful tasks. - Bridges to self-regulated learning and to cognitive load management.  ## Related  - [[wiki/meta-learning/engagement-research|Engagement Research]] — umbrella field - [[wiki/memory/self-regulated-learning|Self-Regulated Learning]] — strategic core - [[

title: ColBERT
description: Late-interaction retriever scoring query-document pairs token-by-token
body_head: # ColBERT  ## Summary ColBERT computes separate token embeddings for query and document, then scores matches with MaxSim over token pairs — a late-interaction design that gets cross-attention quality at near bi-encoder speed. It is a leading model for retrieval and reranking.  ## Details - **Mechanism** — encode the query and each document independently with a transformer, producing a matrix of token embeddings per passage; the relevance score is the sum, over query tokens, of the maximum cosine similarity to any document token (MaxSim); interaction happens at scoring time instead of during encoding, which is why it is called 'late interaction'. - **Deployment** — used both as a first-stag

title: Commitment Devices
description: Structures that bind future behavior to current intentions
body_head: # Commitment Devices  ## Summary  Commitment Devices — Structures that bind future behavior to current intentions. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Devices raise the cost of failing a commitment (money, reputation, deadlines). - Examples: savings locks, public pledges, app blockers. - Effectiveness depends on credibility of the enforcement. - Precommitment is the classic form; temptation bundling is a reward-side variant.  ## Related  - [[wiki/meta-learning/precommitment|Precommitment]] — core form - [[wiki/meta-learning/temptation-bundling|Temptation Bundling]] — incentive variant - [[wiki/memory/self-control-re

title: Communities of Practice
description: Groups bound by shared practice who learn together over time
body_head: # Communities of Practice  ## Summary  Communities of Practice — Groups bound by shared practice who learn together over time.  ## Details  - Communities of practice (Lave & Wenger) are groups of people who share a domain of interest, a set of practices, and a history of mutual engagement — a team of SREs, a research lab, an open-source project. Learning happens through participation, moving from legitimate peripheral participation toward full membership. - Three elements: the domain (shared competence and identity), the community (relationships and mutual engagement), and the practice (shared repertoire of tools, stories, and standards). Knowledge lives in participation more than in docum

title: Competence Need
description: The psychological need to feel effective and capable
body_head: # Competence Need  ## Summary  The competence need is the psychological need to feel effective, capable, and able to master challenges. It is one of the three basic needs in self-determination theory, and it is closely tied to self-efficacy and mastery experiences. Satisfying the competence need matters because it sustains intrinsic motivation, supports skill development, and shapes how people engage with difficulty.  ## Details  - **Definition** — competence is the experience of being effective in interactions with the environment and in valued activities. - **Basic need status** — like autonomy and relatedness, competence is a universal requirement for thriving motivation; its satisfacti

title: Confidence Ratings
description: Expressed probability judgments of one's own answer correctness
body_head: # Confidence Ratings  ## Summary  Confidence Ratings — Expressed probability judgments of one's own answer correctness. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Typically rated 0-100% or on verbal scales; converted for calibration analysis. - Binning answers by confidence reveals over- and underconfidence regions. - Foundation of calibration curves and Brier scores. - Used in retrieval practice to select items for review.  ## Related  - [[wiki/meta-learning/calibration-training|Calibration Training]] — improvement practice - [[wiki/concepts/calibration-curves|Calibration Curves]] — visual analysis - [[wiki/concepts/brier

title: Corrective Feedback Types
description: Kinds of error feedback: confirmation, hints, and explanations
body_head: # Corrective Feedback Types  ## Summary  Corrective Feedback Types — Kinds of error feedback: confirmation, hints, and explanations. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Types range from verification (right/wrong) to elaborated explanations. - Elaborative feedback generally beats verification for conceptual learning. - Timing of explanation matters: after self-generation beats before. - Central design variable for intelligent tutoring systems.  ## Related  - [[wiki/meta-learning/directive-feedback|Directive Feedback]] — direct form - [[wiki/meta-learning/facilitative-feedback|Facilitative Feedback]] — guiding form -

title: Creative Expertise
description: How deliberate practice and domain knowledge support creativity
body_head: # Creative Expertise  ## Summary  Creative Expertise — How deliberate practice and domain knowledge support creativity. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Creativity requires deep domain knowledge plus flexible recombination. - Experts produce more novel and useful ideas in their domain. - Constraints and incubation aid creative work. - Myth of the lone genius; most creative achievement is cumulative.  ## Related  - [[wiki/concepts/conceptual-blending|Conceptual Blending]] — mechanism - [[wiki/memory/deliberate-practice|Deliberate Practice]] — knowledge base - [[wiki/meta-learning/polymath-research|Polymath Researc

title: Cross-Encoder
description: Model scoring query-document pairs jointly through full attention
body_head: # Cross-Encoder  ## Summary A cross-encoder feeds the query and a document together into a transformer and outputs a single relevance score, capturing full token interactions. It is the most accurate but slowest ranking architecture, typically used to rerank top-k candidates.  ## Details - **Mechanism** — `[CLS] query [SEP] doc` through the transformer; the pooled output scores relevance. Because query and document tokens attend to each other in every layer, the model sees exact lexical overlap, negation, paraphrase, and cross-references that independent encodings miss. - **Use pattern** — retrieve 50-100 candidates with a bi-encoder, rerank the top 10 with a cross-encoder; this two-stage

title: Cue-Routine-Reward
description: The three-part behavioral pattern underlying habit formation
body_head: # Cue-Routine-Reward  ## Summary  Cue-Routine-Reward — The three-part behavioral pattern underlying habit formation. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Cues trigger routines that deliver rewards; the loop strengthens with repetition. - Context stability is the strongest predictor of habit formation. - Reward timing and salience shape how quickly the loop consolidates. - Basis of habit-stacking and tiny-habits interventions.  ## Related  - [[wiki/meta-learning/habit-loops|Habit Loops]] — popular framing - [[wiki/meta-learning/habit-stacking|Habit Stacking]] — sequence design - [[wiki/meta-learning/tiny-habits|Tiny H

title: Curiosity-Driven Learning
description: Learning motivated by information gaps and the drive to understand
body_head: # Curiosity-Driven Learning  ## Summary  Curiosity-Driven Learning — Learning motivated by information gaps and the drive to understand.  ## Details  - Curiosity-driven learning is the self-motivated pursuit of knowledge triggered by gaps, novelty, and surprise. Information-gap theory (Loewenstein) frames curiosity as aversive tension between what is known and what is wanted — resolved by acquiring the missing information, which makes the learning intrinsically rewarding. - Empirical work shows curiosity enhances attention, encoding, and memory: information learned during curious states is retained better, partly via dopamine-modulated hippocampal activity. Moderate gaps maximize curiosity

title: Curriculum Learning
description: Training strategy that orders examples from easy to hard, mimicking human learning curricula
body_head: # Curriculum Learning  ## Summary Curriculum learning trains models on easy examples first and gradually introduces harder ones, guided by a difficulty measure and pacing schedule. Bengio et al. showed in 2009 that this ordering can speed convergence and improve generalization. It is the machine-learning mirror of how humans sequence practice in skill acquisition.  ## Details - **Components** — a difficulty scorer (size, noise, model loss), a pacing function (from easy-only to full data), and a schedule policy (fixed, self-paced). - **Why it can help** — starting near the optimum region of the loss landscape can avoid bad local minima; for humans, success builds confidence and schema befor

title: Delay of Gratification
description: Choosing larger later rewards over smaller immediate ones, as in the marshmallow test
body_head: # Delay of Gratification  ## Summary Delay of gratification is the capacity to forgo an immediate reward for a larger future one, famously measured by the marshmallow test. Early correlations with later outcomes were strong but were largely mediated by family background. The construct remains central to goal pursuit and intertemporal choice.  ## Details - **Paradigm** — a child resists one marshmallow to earn two; wait time is the score. The original studies tracked children into adolescence and adulthood, reporting correlations with academic achievement, health, and income that made the task famous as a predictor of life outcomes. - **Reanalyses** — controlling for socioeconomic variables

title: Deliberate Play
description: Playful, self-directed practice that still targets skill development
body_head: # Deliberate Play  ## Summary  Deliberate play is playful, self-directed activity that nevertheless develops skill, combining the motivation of games with the structure of practice. It is contrasted with deliberate practice, which is effortful and externally structured, and with unstructured play, which is fun but less efficient for learning. Deliberate play matters because it sustains engagement and accumulates practice hours, especially for young athletes and musicians.  ## Details  - **Definition** — deliberate play is intrinsically motivated activity with modified rules that keeps tasks fun while exposing performers to relevant challenges. - **Contrast with deliberate practice** — deli

title: Diagnostic Expertise
description: Skilled identification of conditions from evidence
body_head: # Diagnostic Expertise  ## Summary  Diagnostic expertise is the skilled ability to identify conditions, faults, or categories from evidence, as practiced by physicians, mechanics, engineers, and analysts. It combines pattern recognition with deliberate hypothesis testing and is built through extensive, varied, and feedback-rich experience. Diagnostic expertise matters because it determines the quality of high-stakes decisions made under uncertainty. The same evidence can support different conclusions, so expert diagnosis is as much about managing uncertainty as about pattern matching.  ## Details  - **Definition** — diagnostic expertise is the capacity to infer the underlying cause or cate

title: Directive Feedback
description: Feedback that directly tells the learner what is wrong and what to do
body_head: # Directive Feedback  ## Summary  Directive Feedback — Feedback that directly tells the learner what is wrong and what to do. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Directive feedback states the correct answer or the needed correction explicitly. - Efficient for well-defined skills and novice learners. - Risk: bypasses self-correction and reasoning when overused. - Complements error-driven learning by providing the error signal.  ## Related  - [[wiki/meta-learning/corrective-feedback-types|Corrective Feedback Types]] — taxonomy - [[wiki/meta-learning/facilitative-feedback|Facilitative Feedback]] — contrast - [[wiki/met

title: Discovery Learning
description: Learning by actively exploring and finding principles oneself
