body_head: # Discovery Learning  ## Summary  Discovery Learning — Learning by actively exploring and finding principles oneself.  ## Details  - Discovery learning has learners derive principles, rules, or solutions through exploration rather than direct instruction. Bruner's version emphasized structure and intuition; later research tempered the claim — meta-analyses find unguided discovery inferior to guided instruction, while guided discovery with feedback performs well. - The productive core: generating and testing hypotheses creates memorable, transferable understanding; the failure mode is floundering in underdetermined space. - Worked example: given a set of examples and non-examples, a learner

title: Double-Loop Learning
description: Learning that questions governing assumptions, not just corrects errors
body_head: # Double-Loop Learning  ## Summary  Double-Loop Learning — Learning that questions governing assumptions, not just corrects errors.  ## Details  - Argyris & Schön distinguish single-loop learning — detecting and correcting errors within existing assumptions — from double-loop learning, which examines and revises the governing variables themselves. A thermostat is the classic single-loop device: it corrects temperature without questioning the setting; a thermostat that asks whether the target is right is double-loop. - Double-loop learning matters because the most consequential errors are frame errors: optimizing a bad strategy faster does not fix the strategy. It requires surfacing and tes

title: Educational Data Mining
description: Applying data-mining and ML methods to educational data
body_head: # Educational Data Mining  ## Summary  Educational Data Mining — Applying data-mining and ML methods to educational data.  ## Details  - Educational data mining (EDM) applies machine learning and statistics to data from educational systems — answer logs, discussion forums, and clickstreams — to discover patterns and build models of learners and learning. - Typical tasks: knowledge tracing (mastery prediction), student modeling (skill profiles), drop-out prediction, automated essay scoring, and discovering effective learning sequences. Methods include Bayesian networks, factorization machines, sequence mining, and deep networks. - Worked example: mining a million practice sessions reveals t

title: Effort Praise
description: Praising effort and strategy rather than ability
body_head: # Effort Praise  ## Summary  Effort Praise — Praising effort and strategy rather than ability. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Effort praise encourages attributions to controllable causes. - Studies show mixed effects: helpful when paired with strategy guidance, harmful when false. - Best practice: praise specific, effective effort and revise strategy. - Connects to growth-mindset and attribution interventions.  ## Related  - [[wiki/meta-learning/praise-research|Praise Research]] — parent topic - [[wiki/meta-learning/attribution-theory|Attribution Theory]] — mechanism - [[wiki/meta-learning/learned-optimism|Lear

title: Embedding Alignment
description: Mapping embeddings from different spaces or languages into a shared coordinate frame
body_head: # Embedding Alignment  ## Summary Embedding alignment learns a transformation between two embedding spaces — different models, languages, or modalities — so comparable items land near each other. It enables cross-lingual retrieval and model-agnostic vector search.  ## Details - **Approaches** — (1) linear/procrustes alignment from known pairs: given anchor pairs, fit an orthogonal transformation that maps one space onto the other; (2) unsupervised adversarial alignment: train a discriminator to confuse the two spaces without paired anchors; (3) multilingual training: train a single encoder on many languages so alignment is baked in rather than learned post hoc. - **Why it works** — embeddi

title: Emotional Engagement
description: Affective reactions to learning: interest, enjoyment, anxiety, boredom
body_head: # Emotional Engagement  ## Summary  Emotional Engagement — Affective reactions to learning: interest, enjoyment, anxiety, boredom. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Positive emotions foster attention and persistence; negative ones can undermine both. - Emotions interact with cognitive engagement and self-regulation. - Control-value theory links appraisals of control and value to achievement emotions. - Feeds academic-emotions and test-anxiety research.  ## Related  - [[wiki/meta-learning/engagement-research|Engagement Research]] — umbrella field - [[wiki/meta-learning/academic-emotions|Academic Emotions]] — emotio

title: Emotional Regulation
description: Strategies for influencing which emotions arise, when, and how they are expressed
body_head: # Emotional Regulation  ## Summary Emotional regulation is the set of processes that shape emotional experience and expression. Reappraisal (changing interpretation) and distraction are among the most effective strategies; suppression works less well and costs memory. It underpins learning, collaboration, and long-term persistence.  ## Details - **Strategy taxonomy** — Gross's process model orders strategies by when they intervene: situation selection (choosing to avoid a stressful context), situation modification (changing the context), attentional deployment (redirecting attention), cognitive change (reappraising meaning), and response modulation (regulating the outward expression, e.g.,

title: Engagement Research
description: Study of student involvement across behavioral, cognitive, emotional, and agentic dimensions
body_head: # Engagement Research  ## Summary  Engagement Research — Study of student involvement across behavioral, cognitive, emotional, and agentic dimensions. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Engagement is multidimensional: behavior, cognition, emotion, and agency. - Higher engagement predicts achievement, persistence, and well-being. - Engagement is both a process and an outcome, shaped by context and motivation. - Underlies learning-analytics dashboards that track engagement proxies.  ## Related  - [[wiki/meta-learning/behavioral-engagement|Behavioral Engagement]] — dimension - [[wiki/meta-learning/cognitive-engagement

title: Engineering Intuition
description: Expert engineers' gut sense for what will work and what will break
body_head: # Engineering Intuition  ## Summary  Engineering Intuition — Expert engineers' gut sense for what will work and what will break. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Intuition in engineering is compressed experience: pattern-matched cases. - Reliable in familiar territory, dangerous outside it. - Complemented by analysis, testing, and peer review. - Develops through varied projects and post-mortems.  ## Related  - [[wiki/meta-learning/pattern-recognition-expertise|Pattern Recognition Expertise]] — mechanism - [[wiki/episodes/after-action-review|After Action Review]] — development practice - [[wiki/concepts/heuristics

title: Epistemic Curiosity
description: Desire for knowledge that reduces uncertainty and fills understanding gaps
body_head: # Epistemic Curiosity  ## Summary  Epistemic Curiosity — Desire for knowledge that reduces uncertainty and fills understanding gaps. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Epistemic curiosity targets information gaps and drives deep, exploratory learning. - Distinct from perceptual curiosity, which targets novel sensory stimulation. - Information-gap theory: curiosity peaks when the gap between known and unknown is intermediate. - Supports inquiry-based learning and question generation.  ## Related  - [[wiki/meta-learning/perceptual-curiosity|Perceptual Curiosity]] — sensory counterpart - [[wiki/questions/inquiry-cycle

title: Error-Driven Learning
description: Learning by adjusting predictions or behavior in proportion to errors
body_head: # Error-Driven Learning  ## Summary  Error-Driven Learning — Learning by adjusting predictions or behavior in proportion to errors.  ## Details  - Error-driven learning is the family of mechanisms that change a system based on the difference between predicted and actual outcomes. It covers delta-rule and backpropagation learning in connectionist networks, temporal-difference learning in reinforcement learning, and the brain's use of prediction errors (e.g., dopamine signals). - The core insight: learning rate scales with surprise, and errors are information, not just failures. When predictions match outcomes, nothing changes; when they differ, representations and policies update in the dir

title: Expectancy-Value Theory
description: Motivation as the product of success expectations and task value
body_head: # Expectancy-Value Theory  ## Summary  Expectancy-value theory explains motivation and achievement-related choices as the product of two beliefs: the expectation of success and the subjective value of the task. People engage with tasks they believe they can master and that they find intrinsically interesting, useful, important, or worth the cost. The theory matters because it integrates ability beliefs with valuing, predicting course choices, persistence, and performance across domains. Because the two components combine, raising motivation usually requires addressing both beliefs, not just one.  ## Details  - **Definition** — motivated choice depends on expectancy (can I do this?) multipl

title: Experiential Learning
description: Learning through experience transformed by reflection
body_head: # Experiential Learning  ## Summary  Experiential Learning — Learning through experience transformed by reflection.  ## Details  - Experiential learning is learning by doing plus reflecting: Kolb's cycle runs concrete experience → reflective observation → abstract conceptualization → active experimentation, then repeats. Experience without reflection is just activity; reflection without experience is just theory. - Research supports the cycle's value for skill, attitude, and transfer, while noting learners favor different cycle stages (learning styles). The model underlies labs, internships, simulations, and service learning. - Worked example: a student leads a study group (experience), re

title: Expertise Transfer
description: Whether and when skill in one domain carries to another
body_head: # Expertise Transfer  ## Summary  Expertise Transfer — Whether and when skill in one domain carries to another. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Transfer is narrow: expertise is largely domain-specific. - Some components (self-regulation, learning strategies) transfer better than content. - Analogical transfer improves with abstraction and multiple cases. - Important caveat for generalist claims and career pivots.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/transfer-of-learning|Transfer of Learning]] — general phenomenon - [[wiki/meta-learning/narrow-expertise|Narrow Expertise]] — the specificity side - [[wiki/meta-learning/gen

title: Explanation-Based Learning
description: Learning from a single example by explaining why it satisfies a general rule
body_head: # Explanation-Based Learning  ## Summary  Explanation-Based Learning — Learning from a single example by explaining why it satisfies a general rule.  ## Details  - Explanation-based learning (EBL) derives a general rule from a single example plus domain knowledge, by explaining why the example is an instance of a concept. In AI, EBL compiles search experience into general macro-operators; in psychology it parallels the finding that explanatory understanding supports transfer beyond statistical similarity. - EBL trades sample size for prior knowledge: with a good domain theory, one example suffices; without one, it overgeneralizes. Modern deep learning inverts the trade-off, needing many ex

title: Explanatory Style
description: Habitual way people explain good and bad events
body_head: # Explanatory Style  ## Summary  Explanatory style is a person's habitual way of explaining the causes of good and bad events. It is usually described along three dimensions: permanence, pervasiveness, and personalization. The style matters because it shapes emotional reactions, persistence, and motivation: pessimistic explanations for setbacks predict helplessness, while optimistic explanations predict continued effort.  ## Details  - **Definition** — explanatory style captures whether people attribute causes as stable or temporary, global or specific, and internal or external. - **Permanence** — a pessimistic style treats bad events as permanent ("I always fail") while an optimistic styl

title: Facilitative Feedback
description: Feedback that guides learners to discover corrections themselves
body_head: # Facilitative Feedback  ## Summary  Facilitative Feedback — Feedback that guides learners to discover corrections themselves. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Uses hints and questions rather than direct answers. - Slower but builds reasoning and transfer. - Works when learners have enough prior knowledge to bridge the hint. - A key move in scaffolding and Socratic questioning.  ## Related  - [[wiki/meta-learning/corrective-feedback-types|Corrective Feedback Types]] — taxonomy - [[wiki/meta-learning/directive-feedback|Directive Feedback]] — contrast - [[wiki/questions/socratic-questioning|Socratic Questioning]] —

title: Feedback Frequency
description: How often feedback is given and its effects on learning
body_head: # Feedback Frequency  ## Summary  Feedback Frequency — How often feedback is given and its effects on learning. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - High-frequency feedback speeds early gains but can create dependency. - Reducing feedback frequency forces internal error monitoring. - Optimal frequency depends on learner expertise and task difficulty. - Pairs with fading strategies in skill training.  ## Related  - [[wiki/meta-learning/feedback-timing|Feedback Timing]] — when dimension - [[wiki/memory/deliberate-practice|Deliberate Practice]] — feedback-rich practice - [[wiki/meta-learning/self-assessment-accuracy|Sel

title: Feedback Sandwich
description: Framing criticism between positive statements
body_head: # Feedback Sandwich  ## Summary  The feedback sandwich is a communication technique that frames criticism between two positive statements, usually praise, then correction, then closing encouragement. It aims to make corrective feedback more palatable and to preserve the recipient's motivation and self-esteem. The technique is widely taught, though research on its effectiveness is mixed, and it can backfire when praise feels formulaic or the real message is buried.  ## Details  - **Definition** — the sandwich structure is positive feedback, then the critique, then more positive or encouraging feedback. - **Intended function** — the positive layers are meant to reduce defensiveness and keep

title: Feedback Timing
description: When feedback is delivered and how timing affects learning
body_head: # Feedback Timing  ## Summary  Feedback Timing — When feedback is delivered and how timing affects learning. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Immediate feedback helps initial skill acquisition and error correction. - Delayed feedback often benefits retention and transfer after a first attempt. - Timing interacts with task type: motor skills favor immediacy, complex reasoning tolerates delay. - Design choice for tutoring systems and formative assessment.  ## Related  - [[wiki/meta-learning/feedback-frequency|Feedback Frequency]] — adjacent dimension - [[wiki/meta-learning/corrective-feedback-types|Corrective Feedb

title: Feedforward
description: Feedback reframed as guidance for the next attempt
body_head: # Feedforward  ## Summary  Feedforward — Feedback reframed as guidance for the next attempt. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Feedforward states what to do next rather than judging what was done. - Keeps attention on growth and reduces defensiveness. - Works best alongside accurate diagnosis of the past attempt. - Common in coaching and design critique.  ## Related  - [[wiki/meta-learning/coach-feedback|Coach Feedback]] — coaching practice - [[wiki/meta-learning/facilitative-feedback|Facilitative Feedback]] — guiding style - [[wiki/episodes/after-action-review|After Action Review]] — team ritual

title: Fitts-Posner Model
description: Three stages of skill acquisition: cognitive, associative, autonomous
body_head: # Fitts-Posner Model  ## Summary  The Fitts-Posner model describes skill acquisition as a progression through three stages: cognitive, associative, and autonomous. Learners begin with explicit, effortful, error-prone performance and end with fluent, automatic execution requiring little attention. The model matters because it organizes practice design and explains why expertise feels effortless: the cognitive load shifts from the task to higher-level decisions.  ## Details  - **Cognitive stage** — the learner builds a declarative understanding of the task, attends to instructions, and makes frequent errors; performance is slow and conscious. - **Associative stage** — components are refined

title: Flow State
description: Absorbed, effortless engagement when challenge matches skill
body_head: # Flow State  ## Summary  Flow State — Absorbed, effortless engagement when challenge matches skill.  ## Details  - Flow is the state of complete absorption in an activity, marked by intense focus, loss of self-consciousness, distorted time, and intrinsic reward. Csikszentmihalyi's core condition: a balance between perceived challenge and skill, with clear goals and immediate feedback. - Flow matters for learning because it sustains engagement and practice volume; it correlates with enjoyment, creativity, and performance in work, sport, and study. It is fragile: anxiety when challenge exceeds skill, boredom when skill exceeds challenge. - Worked example: a programmer debugging a hard but s

title: Forecasting Research
description: Study of probability estimation about future events and its accuracy
body_head: # Forecasting Research  ## Summary  Forecasting research studies how well people estimate the probability of future events and what improves those estimates. It has found that a small minority of forecasters are consistently better than average, that calibration can be trained, and that structured practices outperform intuition. The research matters because accurate probability judgment underpins decision-making under uncertainty in business, policy, and personal life. Accuracy is measured over many judgments rather than single calls, which is why the research emphasizes calibration statistics and long-run track records.  ## Details  - **Definition** — forecasting research measures the acc

title: Formative Assessment
description: Ongoing assessment used to adjust teaching and learning while it happens
body_head: # Formative Assessment  ## Summary  Formative Assessment — Ongoing assessment used to adjust teaching and learning while it happens.  ## Details  - Formative assessment gathers evidence of learning during instruction to adjust teaching and guide learners — the 'assessment for learning' loop. It contrasts with summative assessment, which certifies learning at the end. Black and Wiliam's review found formative practices among the most effective classroom interventions. - Core moves: share learning intentions, elicit evidence (questions, exit tickets, hinge questions), give feedback that moves learning forward, and activate learners as owners of their progress. - Worked example: a hinge quest

title: Friction Design
description: Deliberately adding or removing effort to shape behavior
body_head: # Friction Design  ## Summary  Friction Design — Deliberately adding or removing effort to shape behavior. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Removing friction (defaults, one-click) raises desired behavior; adding it deters undesired. - Friction includes time, clicks, attention, and cognitive load. - Ethical question: who decides which friction is good. - Core tool of choice-architecture and nudging.  ## Related  - [[wiki/meta-learning/choice-architecture|Choice Architecture]] — framing context - [[wiki/meta-learning/nudges|Nudges]] — application family - [[wiki/meta-learning/tiny-habits|Tiny Habits]] — friction re

title: Future Time Perspective
description: How far and how vividly people project into the future
body_head: # Future Time Perspective  ## Summary  Future time perspective is the degree to which people think about, value, and connect with the future, including how far ahead they project and how vividly they imagine it. It shapes motivation by giving present actions meaning as steps toward future states. The concept matters because a longer, more connected time perspective predicts better planning, delayed gratification, and achievement.  ## Details  - **Definition** — future time perspective covers the extension, content, and connectedness of a person's thoughts about the future. - **Extension** — people differ in how far ahead they typically think, from days to decades, which changes how present

title: Generalist vs Specialist
description: Trade-offs between breadth and depth in knowledge and skill
body_head: # Generalist vs Specialist  ## Summary  Generalist vs Specialist — Trade-offs between breadth and depth in knowledge and skill. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Specialists go deep fast but adapt slowly; generalists flex across domains. - Modern complexity often rewards T-shaped hybrids. - Polymaths contribute via cross-domain analogies. - Choice depends on goals, rate of change, and information access.  ## Related  - [[wiki/meta-learning/narrow-expertise|Narrow Expertise]] — specialist side - [[wiki/meta-learning/t-shaped-skills|T-Shaped Skills]] — hybrid - [[wiki/meta-learning/polymath-research|Polymath Researc

title: GloVe
description: Word embeddings learned from global co-occurrence statistics via matrix factorization
body_head: # GloVe  ## Summary GloVe (Global Vectors) learns word vectors by factorizing a word-word co-occurrence matrix so vector arithmetic reflects co-occurrence ratios. It combined the global statistics view with local-context efficiency.  ## Details - **Mechanism** — weighted least-squares fit over log co-occurrence counts; produces static word vectors. - **Comparison** — word2vec (local windowed sampling) vs GloVe (global counts): similar quality, different training dynamics. - **Legacy** — like word2vec, static and context-free; a baseline for evaluating contextual embeddings.  ## Related - [[wiki/meta-learning/word2vec|Word2Vec]] — the local-context counterpart - [[wiki/data-storage/embeddin

title: Goal Intentions
description: Commitments to achieve particular outcomes
body_head: # Goal Intentions  ## Summary  Goal Intentions — Commitments to achieve particular outcomes. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Goal intentions specify desired outcomes but not when and how to act. - Adding implementation intentions (if-then plans) substantially raises attainment. - Effective goals are specific, challenging, and framed as approach. - Complemented by habit formation for automaticity.  ## Related  - [[wiki/meta-learning/volitional-control|Volitional Control]] — execution support - [[wiki/meta-learning/task-initiation|Task Initiation]] — when goals stall - [[wiki/meta-learning/rubicon-model|Rubicon Mo

title: Grammar Induction
description: Learning the rules of a language from exposure
body_head: # Grammar Induction  ## Summary  Grammar induction is the process of learning the rule system of a language from exposure to its utterances, without being explicitly taught the rules. Learners infer categories, dependencies, and ordering constraints from the statistical structure of the input. The topic matters because it sits at the intersection of language acquisition, statistical learning, and machine learning, and it illuminates how structured knowledge emerges from unstructured experience.  ## Details  - **Definition** — grammar induction is the acquisition of syntactic and morphological regularities from positive examples of a language. - **Statistical foundation** — learners track d

title: Graph Embeddings
description: Low-dimensional vector representations of graph nodes, edges, or subgraphs
body_head: # Graph Embeddings  ## Summary Graph embeddings map nodes (or whole graphs) into vector space so structural similarity becomes geometric proximity. They let standard vector machinery — clustering, similarity search — operate on relational data.  ## Details - **Approaches** — random-walk (node2vec, DeepWalk), matrix factorization (spectral), and message-passing (GNNs). - **Uses** — link prediction, node classification, community detection, and graph retrieval. - **Agent relevance** — embedding mykb's co-occurrence graph would surface structurally similar concepts, complementing text embeddings.  ## Related - [[wiki/meta-learning/node2vec|Node2Vec]] — the canonical random-walk method - [[wik

title: Grit Research
description: Study of perseverance and passion for long-term goals and its predictive power
body_head: # Grit Research  ## Summary Grit research proposes that sustained passion and perseverance predict achievement beyond talent and IQ. Early claims were large; later analyses found modest effects once conscientiousness and demographics are controlled. It remains a useful folk concept and a contested scientific one.  ## Details - **Construct** — Duckworth's two-factor model: consistency of interest (sticking with one goal over years, not flitting between passions) plus perseverance of effort (working hard through setbacks); it is measured by self-report scales and, in some studies, informant reports. - **Predictive power** — early studies reported grit predicting retention at West Point, spel

title: Habit Loops
description: The cue-routine-reward cycle that sustains automatic behavior
body_head: # Habit Loops  ## Summary  Habit Loops — The cue-routine-reward cycle that sustains automatic behavior. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Duhigg's popular framing: cue, routine, reward, plus craving. - Habits form through repetition in consistent contexts. - Design lever: keep cue and reward, change the routine. - Links to cue-routine-reward and habit-stacking practice.  ## Related  - [[wiki/meta-learning/cue-routine-reward|Cue Routine Reward]] — the mechanism - [[wiki/meta-learning/habit-stacking|Habit Stacking]] — building sequences - [[wiki/memory/habit-vs-goal-directed|Habit vs Goal-Directed Control]] — cognit

title: Habit Stacking
description: Anchoring a new habit to an existing routine
body_head: # Habit Stacking  ## Summary  Habit Stacking — Anchoring a new habit to an existing routine. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Formula: after [existing habit], I will [new habit]. - Uses established cues as reliable triggers for new behavior. - Works best when the anchor is genuinely automatic. - A concrete practice from behavior-design books (Clear, Fogg).  ## Related  - [[wiki/meta-learning/cue-routine-reward|Cue Routine Reward]] — mechanism - [[wiki/meta-learning/tiny-habits|Tiny Habits]] — companion method - [[wiki/meta-learning/habit-loops|Habit Loops]] — framework

title: Habit vs Goal-Directed Control
description: Dual-system account of action: automatic stimulus-response habits versus deliberate goal pursuit
body_head: # Habit vs Goal-Directed Control  ## Summary Habit versus goal-directed control distinguishes automatic stimulus-response routines from flexible, outcome-sensitive deliberation. Behavior shifts from goal-directed to habitual with repetition and back when outcomes change. It explains why old habits survive intentions and why environments matter.  ## Details - **Two systems** — model-free (habit) and model-based (goal-directed) action selection: goal-directed control evaluates actions against a learned model of their consequences and flexibly re-plans; habit control stores stimulus-response associations that fire without consulting outcomes, trading flexibility for speed and low cognitive co

title: Identity Development
description: Process of forming a coherent sense of self across adolescence and adulthood
body_head: # Identity Development  ## Summary  Identity development is the lifelong process of forming a coherent sense of who one is, integrating roles, values, and relationships across time. It is most intense during adolescence and young adulthood, when exploration and commitment shape adult identity. Identity matters for learning because it determines what people find meaningful, which goals they pursue, and how they interpret success and failure. Identity is continually revised as life circumstances change, so development does not end in adolescence even though that is when it is most visible.  ## Details  - **Definition** — identity development is the construction of a stable, meaningful self-c

title: Individual Interest
description: Enduring personal preference for and engagement with a domain
body_head: # Individual Interest  ## Summary  Individual Interest — Enduring personal preference for and engagement with a domain. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Individual interest is stable, self-generated, and tied to domain knowledge and values. - Develops from repeated positive situational-interest experiences. - Predicts autonomous practice and deep expertise over time. - Complements identity development and possible-selves research.  ## Related  - [[wiki/meta-learning/interest-theory|Interest Theory]] — parent framework - [[wiki/meta-learning/situational-interest|Situational Interest]] — origin stage - [[wiki/meta-

title: Information-Seeking Behavior
description: Actions people take to acquire, evaluate, and use information
body_head: # Information-Seeking Behavior  ## Summary  Information-Seeking Behavior — Actions people take to acquire, evaluate, and use information. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Models describe need recognition, query formulation, evaluation, and stopping rules. - Cost-benefit trade-offs govern how long people search before satisficing. - Curiosity and uncertainty drive seeking; anxiety can also motivate avoidance. - mykb relevance: gap detection is the system-side mirror of human information seeking.  ## Related  - [[wiki/questions/knowledge-gaps|Knowledge Gaps]] — what triggers seeking - [[wiki/meta-learning/epistemic

title: Inquiry-Based Learning
description: Learning driven by questions, investigation, and evidence
body_head: # Inquiry-Based Learning  ## Summary  Inquiry-Based Learning — Learning driven by questions, investigation, and evidence.  ## Details  - Inquiry-based learning places questions at the center: learners formulate questions, investigate, interpret evidence, and communicate findings. It spans structured inquiry (teacher-chosen questions and methods) through open inquiry (learner-chosen problem and process). - The mechanism is constructivist: knowledge is built through active investigation, with curiosity and ownership sustaining engagement. Evidence shows benefits for conceptual understanding, reasoning, and attitudes, with outcomes dependent on guidance — minimal-guidance versions can flounde

title: Intelligent Tutoring Systems
description: AI-driven tutors that model learners and adapt instruction
body_head: # Intelligent Tutoring Systems  ## Summary  Intelligent Tutoring Systems — AI-driven tutors that model learners and adapt instruction.  ## Details  - Intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) deliver one-on-one-style instruction by modeling the learner, the domain, and pedagogy. Classic architecture: a domain model (expert knowledge), a student model (what the learner knows, often via knowledge tracing), a tutoring model (when to hint, explain, or advance), and an interface. - Evidence: meta-analyses show ITS outperforming traditional classroom instruction in many domains, approaching human tutoring in effect size, especially for well-structured skills like math and programming. - Worked example:

title: Interest Theory
description: How interest develops and drives attention, learning, and persistence
body_head: # Interest Theory  ## Summary  Interest Theory — How interest develops and drives attention, learning, and persistence. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Interest has cognitive (valuing) and affective (enjoyment) components. - Hidi & Renninger's model: triggered situational interest can develop into enduring individual interest. - Interest predicts attention, deep processing, and continued engagement in a domain. - Educational design works to trigger and then cultivate interest.  ## Related  - [[wiki/meta-learning/situational-interest|Situational Interest]] — early stage - [[wiki/meta-learning/individual-interest|

title: Interpreter Training
description: How simultaneous and consecutive interpreters build expertise
body_head: # Interpreter Training  ## Summary  Interpreter Training — How simultaneous and consecutive interpreters build expertise. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Interpreters train working memory, shadowing, and rapid meaning transfer. - Expertise develops over years with deliberate practice and feedback. - Stress and cognitive load are central challenges. - A demanding case of real-time cognitive skill.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/deliberate-practice|Deliberate Practice]] — method - [[wiki/memory/working-memory-capacity|Working Memory Capacity]] — bottleneck - [[wiki/memory/cognitive-load-theory|Cognitive Load Theory]

title: Intrinsic Motivation
description: Engagement driven by interest and enjoyment rather than external reward
body_head: # Intrinsic Motivation  ## Summary  Intrinsic Motivation — Engagement driven by interest and enjoyment rather than external reward.  ## Details  - Intrinsic motivation is doing an activity for its own sake — for interest, enjoyment, or challenge. Self-determination theory grounds it in three basic needs: autonomy, competence, and relatedness; when those are supported, intrinsic motivation thrives; when thwarted, it withers. - Research shows intrinsic motivation predicts deep learning, creativity, persistence, and well-being. Extrinsic rewards can undermine intrinsic motivation for interesting tasks (the overjustification effect), though they can also support it when delivered as informatio

title: Item Response Theory
description: Psychometric models linking item difficulty and ability to response probability
body_head: # Item Response Theory  ## Summary  Item Response Theory — Psychometric models linking item difficulty and ability to response probability.  ## Details  - Item response theory (IRT) models the probability of a correct response as a function of person ability and item parameters. The one-parameter Rasch model varies difficulty only; two- and three-parameter models add discrimination and guessing. - IRT's advantages over raw scores: ability estimates are item-independent (with proper linking), items are characterized independently of the sample, and measurement error is explicit per ability level. It underlies modern adaptive testing. - Worked example: in a CAT, the algorithm selects the nex

title: Knowledge Compilation
description: The stage where separate steps fuse into smooth, single procedures
body_head: # Knowledge Compilation  ## Summary  Knowledge compilation is the stage of skill acquisition in which separate, consciously applied steps fuse into smooth, single procedures. It explains why performance speeds up dramatically as learners practice: the individual components stop being executed one by one and become integrated units. The concept matters because it describes the middle passage of expertise, between initial understanding and full automaticity.  ## Details  - **Definition** — knowledge compilation combines small declarative steps into larger procedural units, reducing the number of separate operations in a task. - **Relation to proceduralization** — proceduralization converts d

title: Knowledge Distillation
description: Training a small student model to imitate a larger teacher model's predictions and knowledge
body_head: # Knowledge Distillation  ## Summary Knowledge distillation transfers a large teacher model's knowledge into a smaller student model by training the student on the teacher's softened output probabilities, not just hard labels. It compresses expensive models for deployment and can even improve small models on target tasks. Hinton, Vinyals and Dean introduced the modern formulation in 2015.  ## Details - **Mechanism** — teacher logits are softened by a temperature parameter; the student minimizes a weighted loss between its distribution and the teacher's, learning dark knowledge such as class similarities. - **Why it works** — probabilities encode more than labels: a teacher's 'cat vs dog' o

title: Knowledge Tracing
description: Modeling whether a learner has mastered a skill from performance history
body_head: # Knowledge Tracing  ## Summary  Knowledge Tracing — Modeling whether a learner has mastered a skill from performance history.  ## Details  - Knowledge tracing estimates a learner's mastery of a skill from their response history. The classic Bayesian knowledge-tracing model (Corbett & Anderson) tracks a latent binary state — mastered or not — with parameters for guess, slip, learning, and initial knowledge, updated after each response. - Modern variants add deep networks (DKVMs), item difficulty, and forgetting. Knowledge tracing powers mastery learning: when mastery probability crosses a threshold, the skill is considered learned and practice moves on. - Worked example: a tutoring system

title: Learned Optimism
description: Seligman's claim that optimistic explanatory styles can be learned
body_head: # Learned Optimism  ## Summary  Learned optimism is the claim, developed by Seligman and colleagues, that the optimistic explanatory style — explaining bad events as temporary, specific, and external and good events as permanent, global, and personal — can be deliberately learned. Because explanatory style shapes persistence, mood, and performance, training it has become an intervention for resilience and wellbeing. The concept matters as a practical bridge from attribution research to behavior change.  ## Details  - **Definition** — learned optimism is the set of skills for interpreting setbacks the way optimists do, disputing pessimistic automatic explanations. - **Theoretical base** — i

title: Learning Analytics
description: Measuring, analyzing, and acting on learning data
body_head: # Learning Analytics  ## Summary  Learning Analytics — Measuring, analyzing, and acting on learning data.  ## Details  - Learning analytics is the collection, measurement, and analysis of learner data — clicks, answers, time, logs — to understand and improve learning. It spans descriptive dashboards, predictive models of at-risk students, and prescriptive recommendations, typically within LMS or adaptive systems. - Value comes from the loop: data → insight → intervention → new data. Predictive models (course completion, mastery) work best when tied to actionable decisions; metrics like time-on-task and quiz mastery are common proxies with real limitations. - Worked example: a dashboard fla

title: Learning Curves
description: Graphs of performance improvement as a function of practice
body_head: # Learning Curves  ## Summary  Learning Curves — Graphs of performance improvement as a function of practice.  ## Details  - Learning curves plot performance (time, errors, success rate) against practice. The typical shape is negatively accelerated: large early gains, diminishing returns later. The power law of practice formalizes this — performance improves as a power function of trials — across perceptual, motor, and cognitive tasks. - Curves are diagnostic: plateaus signal ceiling, fatigue, or a strategy dead-end; step changes signal insight or a new strategy; variability reveals instability. Comparing curves across conditions quantifies training effectiveness. - Worked example: a typis

title: Mastery Experiences
description: Successful performances that build self-efficacy
body_head: # Mastery Experiences  ## Summary  Mastery experiences are successful performances of a task, and they are the most powerful source of self-efficacy. Each genuine success provides direct evidence of capability, especially when the task was challenging and the success required effort. Because efficacy beliefs drive motivation, persistence, and choice, designing opportunities for mastery experiences is a core strategy in learning and coaching. Because mastery experiences act through interpretation, how success is framed and reflected upon shapes how much confidence it builds.  ## Details  - **Definition** — a mastery experience is a firsthand performance of a task that ends in success and is

title: Mastery Goals
description: Goals focused on developing understanding and competence
body_head: # Mastery Goals  ## Summary  Mastery goals are achievement goals oriented toward developing understanding, skill, and genuine competence in a task. Learners pursuing mastery goals measure success against their own progress rather than against others. These goals matter because they consistently predict deeper processing, persistence through difficulty, intrinsic interest, and adaptive responses to failure.  ## Details  - **Definition** — a mastery goal defines success as learning and improvement, so the task itself and one's own growth are the reference points. - **Contrast with performance goals** — performance goals define success as demonstrating ability relative to others, which change

title: Mastery Learning
description: Instruction where learners must reach mastery before advancing
body_head: # Mastery Learning  ## Summary  Mastery Learning — Instruction where learners must reach mastery before advancing.  ## Details  - Mastery learning requires learners to demonstrate mastery of each unit before moving on, with corrective instruction for those who do not. Bloom's model assumes most students can master material if given sufficient time and quality feedback — success becomes a function of opportunity, not fixed aptitude. - Core components: clear objectives, diagnostic assessment, corrective activities for non-masters, enrichment for masters, and a second chance at assessment. Outcomes: higher average achievement and smaller variance between learners, at the cost of pacing flexib

title: Medical Expertise
description: Development of diagnostic and clinical skill in medicine
body_head: # Medical Expertise  ## Summary  Medical Expertise — Development of diagnostic and clinical skill in medicine. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Expert clinicians combine pattern recognition with systematic reasoning. - Diagnostic errors often come from premature closure and bias. - Simulation, feedback, and reflection improve skill. - Domain for studying judgment and decision-making in practice.  ## Related  - [[wiki/meta-learning/diagnostic-expertise|Diagnostic Expertise]] — reasoning side - [[wiki/meta-learning/pattern-recognition-expertise|Pattern Recognition Expertise]] — pattern side - [[wiki/concepts/case-b

title: Model-Based Learning
description: Learning through an explicit internal model of the environment
body_head: # Model-Based Learning  ## Summary  Model-Based Learning — Learning through an explicit internal model of the environment. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Model-based agents build and update a world model, enabling planning and flexible transfer. - Computationally expensive but sample-efficient and robust to change. - In humans, maps the goal-directed control system. - Contrast with model-free learning; hybrid accounts mix both.  ## Related  - [[wiki/meta-learning/model-free-learning|Model-Free Learning]] — counterpart - [[wiki/memory/habit-vs-goal-directed|Habit vs Goal-Directed Control]] — behavioral mapping -

title: Model-Free Learning
description: Learning stimulus-response values directly from experience without a world model
body_head: # Model-Free Learning  ## Summary  Model-Free Learning — Learning stimulus-response values directly from experience without a world model. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Model-free methods cache values from reward history and act reflexively. - Sample-hungry but fast at execution and resistant to planning costs. - Maps onto habitual control in humans. - TD learning and Q-learning are canonical algorithms.  ## Related  - [[wiki/meta-learning/model-based-learning|Model-Based Learning]] — counterpart - [[wiki/meta-learning/reward-prediction-error|Reward Prediction Error]] — learning signal - [[wiki/meta-learning/h

title: Motivation Internalization
description: Process by which externally prompted behaviors become personally endorsed
body_head: # Motivation Internalization  ## Summary  Motivation internalization is the process by which behaviors originally prompted by external pressure become personally endorsed and self-regulated. In self-determination theory, regulation moves along a continuum from external control through introjection and identification to integration. Internalization matters because more internalized motivation predicts more durable engagement, better wellbeing, and more effective self-regulation.  ## Details  - **Definition** — internalization is the progressive taking-in of externally prompted values and behaviors so they feel increasingly like one's own. - **The continuum** — external regulation relies on

title: Motor Learning
description: Acquisition and refinement of movement skills through practice
body_head: # Motor Learning  ## Summary  Motor learning is the process of acquiring and refining movement skills through practice and experience. It produces relatively permanent changes in the capability to perform coordinated actions, from typing and driving to gymnastics and surgery. Motor learning matters because it reveals general principles of practice, feedback, and automaticity that apply to cognitive skill as well.  ## Details  - **Definition** — motor learning is a set of processes associated with practice that lead to relatively permanent changes in the capability for skilled movement. - **Distinction from performance** — temporary performance fluctuations from fatigue, motivation, or atte

title: Musician Practice
description: Practice patterns of expert musicians and their cognitive effects
body_head: # Musician Practice  ## Summary  Musician Practice — Practice patterns of expert musicians and their cognitive effects. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Elite musicians accumulate thousands of hours of deliberate practice. - Practice quality (slow work, error correction) matters more than raw hours. - Musical training shapes auditory, motor, and memory systems. - Model domain for skill-acquisition research.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/deliberate-practice|Deliberate Practice]] — core method - [[wiki/meta-learning/sight-reading-cognition|Sight Reading Cognition]] — sub-skill - [[wiki/memory/dual-coding-theory|Dual

title: Narrow Expertise
description: Deep skill confined to a specific domain or task set
body_head: # Narrow Expertise  ## Summary  Narrow Expertise — Deep skill confined to a specific domain or task set. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Most expertise is narrow: chess skill does not generalize to medicine. - Narrow experts fail when conditions change (inert knowledge). - Value comes from depth; risk from brittleness. - Motivates hybrid generalist-specialist models.  ## Related  - [[wiki/meta-learning/expertise-transfer|Expertise Transfer]] — transfer limits - [[wiki/meta-learning/generalist-vs-specialist|Generalist vs Specialist]] — breadth contrast - [[wiki/meta-learning/t-shaped-skills|T-Shaped Skills]] — co

title: Neuroplasticity
description: The brain's lifelong capacity to reorganize structure and function with experience
body_head: # Neuroplasticity  ## Summary  Neuroplasticity — The brain's lifelong capacity to reorganize structure and function with experience.  ## Details  - Neuroplasticity is the brain's ability to change structurally and functionally in response to experience — the biological substrate of learning and memory. It operates at multiple scales: synaptic strengthening (LTP), dendritic growth, cortical map reorganization, and system-level compensation after injury. - Plasticity is experience-dependent and lifelong, though windows of heightened plasticity (development, post-injury, skill learning) vary by system. The same mechanisms that enable learning enable maladaptive change: addiction and chronic p

title: Node2Vec
description: Random-walk method learning node embeddings that balance homophily and structural roles
body_head: # Node2Vec  ## Summary Node2Vec learns node embeddings by simulating biased random walks and feeding them to a word2vec-style model. Its two walk parameters, p (return) and q (in-out), let it interpolate between community-focused and role-focused embeddings.  ## Details - **Mechanism** — second-order random walks sample node neighborhoods: from each node, walkers take biased steps guided by p and q, generating sequences that act as 'sentences'; skip-gram with negative sampling learns vectors from these walk sequences, so nodes that appear in similar walk contexts land near each other. - **Parameters** — p controls the likelihood of immediately returning to the previous node (low p keeps wa

title: Novelty Detection
description: Cognitive and computational processes that flag inputs as new or unexpected
body_head: # Novelty Detection  ## Summary Novelty detection is the brain's fast tagging of stimuli as new relative to stored knowledge. Novelty grabs attention, boosts encoding, and motivates exploration. Systems from intrusion detection to knowledge curation implement the same idea algorithmically.  ## Details - **Neural basis** — hippocampus and midbrain respond to novelty with enhanced encoding. - **Behavior** — novelty seeking and curiosity follow detection. - **Computational use** — anomaly and outlier detection models. - **In mykb** — dedup and gap detection flag novel versus known content.  ## Related - [[wiki/meta-learning/novelty-seeking|Novelty Seeking]] — the motivational response - [[wik

title: Novelty Seeking
description: Drive to explore unfamiliar stimuli, situations, and ideas
body_head: # Novelty Seeking  ## Summary  Novelty Seeking — Drive to explore unfamiliar stimuli, situations, and ideas. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Novelty activates dopaminergic reward circuitry and motivates exploration. - Balanced with safety and exploitation; excessive novelty seeking links to impulsivity. - Educational value: novel contexts raise attention and curiosity. - Underlies curiosity-driven learning and information-seeking behavior.  ## Related  - [[wiki/meta-learning/perceptual-curiosity|Perceptual Curiosity]] — sensory form - [[wiki/meta-learning/intrinsic-motivation|Intrinsic Motivation]] — motivationa

title: Nudges
description: Low-cost design changes that steer behavior while preserving choice
body_head: # Nudges  ## Summary  Nudges — Low-cost design changes that steer behavior while preserving choice. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Nudges alter the choice environment, not incentives or mandates. - Examples: defaults, reminders, social proof, salience. - Effect sizes vary; replication is uneven across contexts. - Raise design and ethics questions for personal systems like mykb.  ## Related  - [[wiki/meta-learning/choice-architecture|Choice Architecture]] — design discipline - [[wiki/meta-learning/social-accountability|Social Accountability]] — norm-based nudge - [[wiki/concepts/decision-quality|Decision Quality

title: Organizational Learning
description: How organizations acquire, retain, and apply knowledge as collective entities
body_head: # Organizational Learning  ## Summary  Organizational Learning — How organizations acquire, retain, and apply knowledge as collective entities.  ## Details  - Organizational learning is the capacity of an organization to improve through the acquisition, distribution, interpretation, and retention of knowledge. It operates through individuals but persists in routines, documents, culture, and systems — knowledge that outlives any member. - Argyris & Schön distinguished single-loop learning (fixing errors within existing frames) from double-loop learning (questioning the frames themselves). Barriers include success traps, defensive routines, and knowledge transfer failures across teams and ti

title: Outcome Expectancy
description: Belief that a behavior will produce a given outcome
body_head: # Outcome Expectancy  ## Summary  Outcome expectancy is the belief that a behavior will produce a particular outcome or consequence. It is distinct from self-efficacy: efficacy concerns whether one can perform the behavior, while outcome expectancy concerns what the behavior will yield. Both beliefs matter for motivation, because people pursue actions they think they can do and that they expect to lead to valued results.  ## Details  - **Definition** — outcome expectancy is a judgment about the causal link between an action and its results, ranging from physical to social and self-evaluative outcomes. - **Distinction from efficacy** — a person may be confident they can exercise (high effic

title: Pattern Recognition Expertise
description: Experts' ability to see meaningful patterns novices miss
body_head: # Pattern Recognition Expertise  ## Summary  Pattern Recognition Expertise — Experts' ability to see meaningful patterns novices miss. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Experts chunk information into larger, meaningful units (chess positions, X-rays). - Perceptual learning tunes feature extraction over thousands of examples. - Enables rapid, accurate situation assessment. - Root of intuition and of narrow-expertise effects.  ## Related  - [[wiki/meta-learning/perceptual-expertise|Perceptual Expertise]] — perceptual side - [[wiki/meta-learning/chess-expertise|Chess Expertise]] — classic case - [[wiki/memory/chunkin

title: Pattern Recognition Learning
description: Acquiring the ability to classify and respond to recurring patterns
body_head: # Pattern Recognition Learning  ## Summary  Pattern recognition learning is the acquisition of the ability to classify and respond appropriately to recurring patterns in the environment. From reading words to diagnosing diseases, experts are distinguished by their refined pattern libraries. The concept matters because pattern recognition is the foundation of expertise: it converts repeated experience into fast, accurate, and largely automatic classification. Recognition speed and accuracy improve with the quantity and variety of examples, which is why exposure-rich domains produce the most fluent experts.  ## Details  - **Definition** — pattern recognition learning is the process of extrac

title: Peer Assessment
description: Learners evaluating each other's work against criteria
body_head: # Peer Assessment  ## Summary  Peer assessment is a practice in which learners evaluate each other's work against explicit criteria, providing feedback and often grades. It is used in classrooms and online courses to scale feedback, deepen understanding of quality standards, and develop evaluative judgment. Peer assessment matters because giving feedback can teach as much as receiving it, and because it develops the self-assessment skills learners need for independent learning. The reliability of peer assessment depends heavily on design: clear criteria, training, and calibration convert peer judgment from noise into useful signal.  ## Details  - **Definition** — peer assessment involves l

title: Perceptual Curiosity
description: Drive for novel sensory stimulation and surprise
body_head: # Perceptual Curiosity  ## Summary  Perceptual Curiosity — Drive for novel sensory stimulation and surprise. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Perceptual curiosity motivates exploration of new sights, sounds, and environments. - Thought to be rooted in arousal and novelty detection. - Shorter-lived than epistemic curiosity, which sustains longer inquiry. - Animal research on novelty-seeking informs the human account.  ## Related  - [[wiki/meta-learning/epistemic-curiosity|Epistemic Curiosity]] — knowledge-based counterpart - [[wiki/meta-learning/novelty-seeking|Novelty Seeking]] — broader drive - [[wiki/concepts/n

title: Perceptual Expertise
description: Expert-level discrimination and recognition within a visual domain
body_head: # Perceptual Expertise  ## Summary  Perceptual Expertise — Expert-level discrimination and recognition within a visual domain. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Experts (radiologists, birders, fingerprint examiners) discriminate subtle differences. - Develops via exposure, feedback, and motivation over years. - Neural tuning: fusiform specialization for the expert domain. - Faces limits when the domain changes.  ## Related  - [[wiki/meta-learning/pattern-recognition-expertise|Pattern Recognition Expertise]] — general process - [[wiki/meta-learning/medical-expertise|Medical Expertise]] — professional case - [[wiki/

title: Performance Goals
description: Goals focused on demonstrating competence relative to others
body_head: # Performance Goals  ## Summary  Performance goals are achievement goals focused on demonstrating competence relative to others rather than on developing understanding. Learners with performance goals aim to look capable, outperform peers, or avoid looking incapable. These goals matter because they shape how learners respond to difficulty, feedback, and failure, sometimes supporting short-term achievement but often undermining deep learning and resilience.  ## Details  - **Definition** — a performance goal defines success as proving ability, with others' performance as the reference point. - **Approach and avoidance** — performance-approach goals seek to demonstrate superiority, while perf

title: Personalized Learning
description: Instruction tailored to individual learners' needs, pace, and interests
body_head: # Personalized Learning  ## Summary  Personalized Learning — Instruction tailored to individual learners' needs, pace, and interests.  ## Details  - Personalized learning tailors content, pace, and pedagogy to each learner — by hand in tutoring and small classes, by algorithm in adaptive platforms. It rests on two claims: learners differ in readiness and interests, and instruction that matches those differences works better than uniform instruction. - Evidence is mixed: well-implemented personalization (competency-based pacing, learner choice, adaptive practice) shows positive effects; superficial personalization (only pace changes) shows little. The mechanism is better targeting of ZPD an

title: Polymath Research
description: Study of multi-domain expertise and its cognitive basis
body_head: # Polymath Research  ## Summary  Polymath Research — Study of multi-domain expertise and its cognitive basis. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Polymaths achieve expertise in multiple fields, often linked by shared structure. - Cross-domain analogy and transfer are hypothesized mechanisms. - Rare: depth in one domain already requires thousands of hours. - Relevant to curiosity-driven learning and knowledge integration.  ## Related  - [[wiki/meta-learning/generalist-vs-specialist|Generalist vs Specialist]] — breadth framing - [[wiki/concepts/analogical-transfer|Analogical Transfer]] — mechanism - [[wiki/meta-learni

title: Possible Selves
description: Mental representations of who one might become
body_head: # Possible Selves  ## Summary  Possible selves are mental representations of who one might become: the hoped-for, feared, and expected selves that guide motivation and identity. They project the self into the future and give current behavior direction and meaning. Possible selves matter because vivid, accessible self-images influence goal pursuit, self-regulation, and the choices people make about learning and life.  ## Details  - **Definition** — possible selves are future-oriented components of the self-concept, including versions of the self one hopes to become, expects to become, or fears becoming. - **Motivational function** — hoped-for selves pull behavior forward while feared selves

title: Posttraumatic Growth
description: Positive psychological change reported after struggling with highly challenging life events
body_head: # Posttraumatic Growth  ## Summary Posttraumatic growth refers to reported improvements in relationships, appreciation of life, personal strength, spirituality, and new possibilities after adversity. It is distinct from resilience and from mere recovery. Reported growth is real, but it coexists with ongoing distress and can be overstated.  ## Details - **Domains** — Tedeschi & Calhoun's five-factor model: improved relationships (deeper, more honest connections), increased appreciation of life, a sense of personal strength ('if I survived that, I can handle this'), new possibilities or changed life direction, and spiritual/existential development; the Posttraumatic Growth Inventory measures

title: Power Law of Practice
description: The regular finding that performance improves as a power function of practice
body_head: # Power Law of Practice  ## Summary  Power Law of Practice — The regular finding that performance improves as a power function of practice.  ## Details  - The power law of practice (Newell & Rosenbloom) states that response time or error rate decreases as a power function of the number of practice trials: T = a × N^b. Improvement is rapid at first and slows with practice, with b typically between -0.5 and -1 across many tasks. - The law holds across domains — typing, motor skills, mental arithmetic, reading — and motivated cognitive architectures like ACT-R, where it emerges from chunking and production strengthening. Log-log plots of performance versus trials approximate straight lines. -

title: Praise Research
description: Evidence on how praise affects motivation and learning
body_head: # Praise Research  ## Summary  Praise Research — Evidence on how praise affects motivation and learning. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Praise type matters more than amount: process praise beats person praise. - Effort praise can backfire if it implies low ability. - Sincere, specific, and informational praise supports intrinsic motivation. - Foundational to mindset and attribution research.  ## Related  - [[wiki/meta-learning/effort-praise|Effort Praise]] — specific type - [[wiki/meta-learning/attribution-theory|Attribution Theory]] — interpretation mechanism - [[wiki/meta-learning/verbal-persuasion|Verbal Per

title: Precommitment
description: Binding oneself in advance to resist future temptation
body_head: # Precommitment  ## Summary  Precommitment — Binding oneself in advance to resist future temptation. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Classic examples: Ulysses and the Sirens, Christmas savings accounts. - Works by removing the tempting option or raising its cost. - Strongest when the constraint is hard to reverse. - Foundational strategy in behavioral self-control research.  ## Related  - [[wiki/meta-learning/commitment-devices|Commitment Devices]] — device family - [[wiki/memory/delay-of-gratification|Delay of Gratification]] — goal - [[wiki/memory/self-control-research|Self-Control Research]] — evidence base

title: Prediction Error Signal
description: Neural and computational signal encoding the gap between expected and actual outcomes
body_head: # Prediction Error Signal  ## Summary Prediction error is the difference between expected and received reward, and the brain broadcasts it via dopamine to drive learning. Positive errors reinforce; negative errors update expectations downward. It is the computational core of reinforcement learning and of curiosity-driven exploration.  ## Details - **Rescorla-Wagner legacy** — errors gate associative learning. - **Dopamine** — phasic firing encodes reward prediction error. - **Modern RL** — TD-learning algorithms use the same signal. - **In mykb** — treat outcome surprises as update triggers, not noise.  ## Related - [[wiki/meta-learning/error-driven-learning|Error-Driven Learning]] — the l

title: Problem-Based Learning
description: Learning organized around solving authentic problems
body_head: # Problem-Based Learning  ## Summary  Problem-Based Learning — Learning organized around solving authentic problems.  ## Details  - Problem-based learning (PBL) organizes curriculum around authentic problems: learners encounter a problem first, identify what they need to know, study, and return to apply their learning. Originating in medical education (McMaster), it spread across professions and schools. - Claimed mechanisms: activation of prior knowledge, relevance-driven motivation, elaboration through discussion, and transfer via contextualized practice. Evidence: PBL improves problem-solving and application; its effect on basic knowledge is mixed versus lecture. - Worked example: a cas

title: Proceduralization
description: Converting declarative knowledge into procedural skill
body_head: # Proceduralization  ## Summary  Proceduralization is the process by which declarative knowledge — knowing that — is converted into procedural skill — knowing how. In cognitive architectures such as ACT-R, repeated application of facts and rules compiles them into productions that run quickly and without conscious recall. Proceduralization matters because it explains the transition from halting, deliberate performance to fluent expertise.  ## Details  - **Definition** — proceduralization transforms explicit, verbally accessible knowledge into condition-action rules that can fire automatically. - **ACT-R account** — in ACT-R, declarative chunks are encoded in memory, and with practice they

title: Procrastination Research
description: Study of voluntary delay of intended action despite expected costs
body_head: # Procrastination Research  ## Summary  Procrastination Research — Study of voluntary delay of intended action despite expected costs. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Procrastination is a self-regulation failure, not a time-management skill gap. - Trait procrastination correlates with impulsivity and weaker conscientiousness. - Interventions: implementation intentions, environment design, and self-compassion. - Explained formally by temporal motivation theory.  ## Related  - [[wiki/meta-learning/temporal-motivation-theory|Temporal Motivation Theory]] — formal account - [[wiki/meta-learning/task-initiation|Task I

title: Project-Based Learning
description: Learning through sustained projects that produce authentic artifacts
body_head: # Project-Based Learning  ## Summary  Project-Based Learning — Learning through sustained projects that produce authentic artifacts.  ## Details  - Project-based learning (PBL) organizes learning around extended projects that produce a real artifact — a report, model, product, or performance. It combines inquiry, collaboration, and reflection, usually anchored by a driving question. - Evidence: meta-analyses find positive effects on content knowledge, collaboration, and engagement, with quality depending on project design, feedback, and time. Key design features: authentic problem, student voice, sustained inquiry, critique, and public product. - Worked example: a course asks teams to desi

title: Purposeful Practice
description: Practice with clear goals, feedback, and comfort-zone stretching, short of full deliberate practice
body_head: # Purposeful Practice  ## Summary  Purposeful Practice — Practice with clear goals, feedback, and comfort-zone stretching, short of full deliberate practice. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Ericsson's ladder: naive → purposeful → deliberate practice. - Purposeful practice has specific goals, focused attention, and feedback. - Missing element vs deliberate: expert-designed training methods. - A practical target for self-directed learners.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/deliberate-practice|Deliberate Practice]] — top of the ladder - [[wiki/meta-learning/coach-feedback|Coach Feedback]] — feedback source - [[wiki/meta

title: Reflective Practice
description: Systematically examining one's own experience and actions to improve
body_head: # Reflective Practice  ## Summary  Reflective Practice — Systematically examining one's own experience and actions to improve.  ## Details  - Reflective practice is the disciplined review of experience — what happened, what was assumed, what worked — to improve future action. Schön framed professionals as 'reflective practitioners' who think in action and reflect on action, against the model of technical rationality. - Models structure the cycle: Kolb (experience → reflection → conceptualization → experimentation), Gibbs (description, feelings, evaluation, analysis, conclusion, action plan), and Rolfe's 'what, so what, now what'. Reflection is most valuable when evidence-based and action-b

title: Relatedness Need
description: The psychological need for connection and belonging
body_head: # Relatedness Need  ## Summary  The relatedness need is the psychological need to feel connected to others, to belong, and to be cared for. It is one of the three basic psychological needs in self-determination theory, alongside autonomy and competence. The need matters because its satisfaction predicts engagement, wellbeing, and persistence, and its frustration predicts disengagement and ill-being, especially for learners who feel marginalized.  ## Details  - **Definition** — relatedness is the experience of being meaningfully connected to others and feeling that one matters to them. - **Basic need status** — like autonomy and competence, relatedness is considered a universal nutrient for

title: Resilience Research
description: Study of adaptation and recovery in the face of adversity, stress, and failure
body_head: # Resilience Research  ## Summary Resilience research examines why some people bounce back from setbacks while others languish. Findings emphasize modifiable factors: social support, cognitive reappraisal, routines, and growth framing. Resilience is a process, not a fixed trait, and it is trainable.  ## Details - **Process view** — resilience is adaptation over time, not absence of distress: momentary reactions (anxiety, anger, grief) are normal, and what distinguishes resilient trajectories is recovery speed and the eventual return of functioning, not the lack of pain; measuring a single timepoint misclassifies many people. - **Protective factors** — the most replicated predictors are rel

title: Reward Prediction Error
description: Difference between expected and received reward, the signal driving reinforcement learning
body_head: # Reward Prediction Error  ## Summary  Reward Prediction Error — Difference between expected and received reward, the signal driving reinforcement learning.  ## Details  - Reward prediction error (RPE) is the difference between received and expected reward. Schultz's recordings of midbrain dopamine neurons showed phasic firing for unexpected rewards, suppression when expected rewards are omitted, and transfer to reward-predicting cues — the signature of a temporal-difference learning signal. - RPEs drive learning in model-free reinforcement learning: values update toward observed outcomes, so behavior adapts to changing contingencies. Positive RPEs reinforce, negative RPEs punish and promo

title: Risk Literacy
description: Ability to interpret risk information and make informed decisions
body_head: # Risk Literacy  ## Summary  Risk literacy is the ability to interpret risk information and use it to make informed decisions under uncertainty. It covers understanding probabilities, comparing risks, and resisting misleading presentations of numbers. The concept matters because poor risk literacy leads to systematic misjudgments in health, finance, and everyday life, and because how risk information is presented can either support or undermine good decisions.  ## Details  - **Definition** — risk literacy involves reading, evaluating, and acting on quantitative statements about uncertain outcomes. - **Natural frequencies** — presenting risks as natural frequencies ("10 out of 1,000") rathe

title: Rubicon Model
description: Heckhausen's phase model separating deliberation from volitional implementation
body_head: # Rubicon Model  ## Summary  Rubicon Model — Heckhausen's phase model separating deliberation from volitional implementation. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Four phases: predecisional deliberation, preactional planning, actional implementation, postactional evaluation. - Crossing the rubicon = committing to a goal and switching to implementation mindset. - Explains why post-commitment information is processed differently. - Useful for designing decision and planning systems.  ## Related  - [[wiki/meta-learning/goal-intentions|Goal Intentions]] — commitment content - [[wiki/meta-learning/volitional-control|Volit

title: Scaffolding Learning
description: Temporary support that lets learners do more than they could alone, then fades
body_head: # Scaffolding Learning  ## Summary  Scaffolding Learning — Temporary support that lets learners do more than they could alone, then fades.  ## Details  - Scaffolding is structured assistance — hints, prompts, partial solutions, worked examples — that enables learners to perform just beyond their independent ability, with the support removed as competence grows. The concept extends Vygotsky's ZPD into a design principle. - Effective scaffolds are contingent (more help when struggling, less when succeeding), fading, and transferred to the learner's own strategies. Over-scaffolding creates dependency; under-scaffolding abandons the learner to frustration. - Worked example: solving a physics p

title: Self-Assessment Accuracy
description: How well learners judge their own performance and knowledge
body_head: # Self-Assessment Accuracy  ## Summary  Self-Assessment Accuracy — How well learners judge their own performance and knowledge. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - People are overconfident on average; accuracy improves with feedback and calibration training. - Self-assessment is more accurate for well-known domains and after practice tests. - Incentives reduce but do not eliminate bias. - Foundational to calibration-of-judgment and self-regulated learning.  ## Related  - [[wiki/memory/metacognition-and-monitoring|Metacognition and Monitoring]] — parent capacity - [[wiki/meta-learning/calibration-training|Calibration

title: Self-Concept Research
description: How self-perceptions form and relate to achievement
body_head: # Self-Concept Research  ## Summary  Self-concept research investigates how people form and maintain perceptions of themselves and how those perceptions relate to achievement and wellbeing. A central finding is that self-concept is multidimensional and domain-specific, with academic self-concept tied closely to performance in particular subjects. The research matters because self-perceptions influence motivation, effort, and the interpretation of feedback, creating self-fulfilling cycles.  ## Details  - **Definition** — self-concept is the organized set of beliefs a person holds about their own attributes, abilities, and roles. - **Multidimensional structure** — self-concept separates into

title: Self-Control Research
description: Empirical study of resisting temptation, regulating impulses, and predicting life outcomes
body_head: # Self-Control Research  ## Summary Self-control research measures the ability to override impulses in favor of longer-term goals and links it to outcomes like health, grades, and finances. Trait measures predict real-world behavior better than lab tasks do. Interventions shift the environment more reliably than they strengthen the trait.  ## Details - **Measurement gap** — questionnaires (trait self-control scales) and behavioral tasks (stop-signal, delay discounting, marshmallow-type tasks) correlate only weakly with each other, and each predicts different outcomes: trait measures predict long-term life outcomes like health and financial stability, while lab tasks predict immediate task

title: Self-Determination Theory
description: Motivation theory centered on autonomy, competence, and relatedness needs
body_head: # Self-Determination Theory  ## Summary  Self-Determination Theory — Motivation theory centered on autonomy, competence, and relatedness needs. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Deci & Ryan: intrinsic motivation thrives when autonomy, competence, and relatedness are supported. - Motivation ranges from amotivation through extrinsic regulation to intrinsic motivation on a continuum.  ## Related  - [[wiki/meta-learning/autonomy-support|Autonomy Support]] — need-satisfying practice - [[wiki/meta-learning/competence-need|Competence Need]] — second need - [[wiki/meta-learning/relatedness-need|Relatedness Need]] — third

title: Self-Grading
description: Learners scoring their own work against model answers
